Its **Experiments** tab works as the mouse colony's does, for your animals, groups and cohorts, and can start with a housing's animals: see [Experiments](https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments).

### Troubleshooting

#### A colleague's database isn't in my sidebar

It may be their personal one (*Just you* on its tile), which only they and admins see, or an admin may have switched it off.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/any-organism

---

## Plasmids

Plasmid records with their sequence and map, and the box each tube is in.

### What this does for your cloning

A construct is only as good as what you can still prove about it a year later: what it was built from, which primers made it, which tube in the freezer is the real one, and whether the sequence in the file is the sequence in the tube. These pages keep the whole loop in one place instead of across SnapGene files, a primer spreadsheet and a box diagram.

| Designing it | **Assemble a plasmid** builds the next construct out of the ones you already have — digest and ligate, Gibson or Golden Gate — and the product records what it was made from, so a year later the family tree answers the question instead of your memory. |
|---|---|
| The primers it needs | Primers the wizard designs, and any you draw on a map yourself, land in the lab's **Primers** database marked *to order*, with the plasmid beside them. Tick them and **Copy for ordering** hands the list to your supplier — after **Find saved primers** has shown any the lab already has that bind. |
| Checking what you got | **Verify sequencing** checks the Sanger reads of each clone against the map and names every base that differs, and what it does to the protein; **Detect features** marks the lab's known elements on a new map, and the reads that confirmed the clone live on the plasmid itself under **Files**, with the gel photo. |
| Finding the tube | Every plasmid has a box position, and the bacteria carrying it sit in **Glycerol stocks** with their own box — so "which tube" has an answer that is not a colleague's memory. |
| Handing it on | A virus made from it names the plasmid; the plasmid's page lists what was made from it. Download it as GenBank whenever someone outside the lab asks. |

What you stop doing: keeping maps in one folder and primers in another spreadsheet, retyping a primer to order it, guessing which miniprep is the good one, and losing what a construct was built from when the person who built it leaves.

- At the top, tabs for the databases that go with plasmids — **Primers**, **Glycerol stocks**, **Viruses** — in the order the work runs. Each is an ordinary database with its own sheet ([see them](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders)); they share one place in the sidebar, **Molecular biology** (just **Plasmids** while the lab has none of them), because each names the plasmid it came from.

### The plasmid sheet

- Show them as a **Table**, by storage **Boxes**, or as a **List**; chips for *Mine*, *Has sequence*, *In a box*.

- **Sequence**, beside each plasmid's number in the table, opens its sequence and map (**Add sequence** when it has none yet); the number opens the same page.

- **New plasmid** takes a name, backbone, insert, resistance, owner and a box position (blank takes the next free one) — or paste a list of names to make several. Drop in a SnapGene `.dna`, GenBank, FASTA or plain-text sequence: its name, features and every annotation note come with it, and a file of several sequences keeps the first and says so.

### The sequence and its map

- Open a plasmid to see its sequence and features on an interactive map you can edit (edits save themselves), full screen if you like. **Download** above the map gives it as GenBank (with every feature) or FASTA. **Versions**, below the map, lists every earlier sequence (replaced, cleared or edited) with **Restore**. **Storage** and **Properties** are the other tabs. On **Properties**, **Made from** records its backbone, insert or template (a plasmid in the lab, by number or name, or one from outside it such as *Addgene #11150*) and how it was made; the page then shows **Made from** and **Used to make** above the map, and a **Family tree** both ways. **Storage** also lists its [glycerol stocks](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders), with the box each is in, and the viruses made from it ([Viruses](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders)). Its address carries its number: plasmid #12 is `…/plasmid/12`.

*A plasmid map*

### Knowing what a sequence holds

- The **Feature library** (a link at the top of Plasmids) keeps the lab's elements by sequence: promoters, ITRs and LTRs, WPRE, resistance genes, tags. **Add to library**, above a well-annotated map (a SnapGene or Addgene file, say), keeps its named features there; an admin can **Collect from every plasmid**. On the library page, **Read elements from files** takes them straight from annotated files — the GenBank a repository gives you, a SnapGene `.dna`, a vendor's map — several at once, without making a plasmid for each. Nothing is built in: every element is one your own files carry, because a sequence typed from memory and wrong by one base would mislabel every map in the lab. An admin can also fetch the **common-features pack** — about 1,900 elements curated from some 2,000 widely used plasmids, downloaded from the open research archive when you ask for it (about a minute; the page shows it when it is in). Its authors built it by exporting a commercial program's published library, so check anything you rely on; elements you added yourself always win over it. Search the library by name or by sequence. On any other plasmid, **Detect features** marks each library element wherever it is, on either strand and across the origin, and keeps the map as it was in **Versions**.

- If your lab runs a server, whoever looks after it can install **pLannotate** (a separate, free program) and **Annotate with pLannotate** then appears above the map. It finds elements by comparing sequences rather than matching them exactly, so it catches a codon-optimised gene or a promoter a base or two off, which the library on its own will miss. Everything it marks is kept in **Versions**, so it can be undone.

### Building a new plasmid

- **Assemble a plasmid**, from the top of Plasmids or from above any map, builds the next plasmid out of the ones you have. Fill the tray with fragments — a whole plasmid, one of its features, a region between two bases, or a piece an enzyme leaves — in the order they go together, turning any of them round, and put them together three ways: **digest and ligate** (cut with the same enzymes and let the sticky ends meet), **Gibson / NEBuilder HiFi** (neighbouring fragments share twenty-odd bases where they meet; the wizard designs the primers that add them, each with its melting temperature) or **Golden Gate** (BsaI, BsmBI or BbsI, which cut outside their own site, so every junction is a four-base overhang you chose). When you cut a plasmid, only the enzymes that actually have a site in it are offered, with how many sites each has and the single cutters first, and the piece you pick is drawn on a ring of the plasmid it came off, so you can see which part comes out before you take it. Each junction shows its own bases, and one line tells you what is wrong and which end it is — *Fragment 2's 3′ end has no overlap with fragment 3* — rather than that it did not work. A Golden Gate is refused when two junctions take the same overhang, when one is another backwards, or when one reads the same on both strands, because each of those puts the pieces together in more than one way. You see the product's map, its length and every fragment in it before anything is made. **Create the plasmid** then makes an ordinary plasmid: the features of each fragment at their new places (a feature a cut runs through keeps the part that is there, and says so), each fragment marked on the map so you can see the joins, **Made from** filled in for every plasmid it came out of with the enzymes and coordinates used, the first entry in its **Versions**, and the library's elements marked if you asked. A Gibson's primers are saved in the [Primers](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders) database marked *to order* and drawn on the map of the plasmid each one amplifies, so **Copy for ordering** picks them up with the rest.

- A primer you draw on the map (select bases, then **Edit → Create → Primer**) is also kept in the lab's [Primers](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders) database, marked *to order*, with the plasmid in its **Plasmid** column. The **Primers** card under the map lists every primer for this plasmid, where it binds and any 5′ tail; tick some, then **Copy for ordering** (name and sequence, one per line, to paste into a supplier's form) or **Export for ordering** (a CSV).

- Before you order a new primer, turn on **Find saved primers** on that card. It looks through every primer saved in the Primers databases you can see — whichever plasmid they were made for — and lists each one that binds this sequence: where, on which strand, and whether it is an *exact match* or matches only at its 3′ end with a 5′ tail (a restriction site, a homology arm, or a few bases that differ). Its name opens the primer, so you can see whether there is still a tube. **Show on map** draws them on the map in amber, to look at; they are not saved with the plasmid, and editing the map while they are shown leaves them out. A primer only counts if at least its last 15 bases match exactly. The same switch is on the read-only map that a glycerol stock or virus opens.

### Checking a clone's sequencing

- **Verify sequencing**, below the map, checks Sanger reads of a miniprep or clone against this plasmid. Choose the reads — the `.ab1` chromatograms the sequencing service sends, or FASTA or text files — or paste the bases under **Paste reads instead**; reads already kept under **Files** can be ticked to check again. Press **Verify**.

- Each read's poor ends are trimmed by its own quality values, then the read is placed on the map, whichever strand it was read from and across the origin of a circular plasmid, and compared base by base. You get one line for the clone — *Matches the map across 425–1,359, covering EGFP*, or *1 difference from the map: C→A at 740 in EGFP (A14D)* — a strip showing where each read lies over the map's features with every difference marked in red, a line for each read (strand, the bases it covers, how much of it agrees), and a table of the differences: the position, the change, the features it falls in, what it does to a coding sequence (*silent*, an amino-acid change such as *A14D*, a stop codon, or a frameshift), the read's quality there, how many of the reads covering that base show it, and, for an `.ab1`, the stretch of trace around it, the base in question shaded.

- A difference where the read's quality is below 20 is greyed and called a likely sequencing error: look at its trace, or read that stretch again from the other strand. A read that doesn't match the plasmid at all is said too, as is one that follows the map only partway (an insert, a deletion, or the wrong plasmid).

- A chromatogram with a second peak under many of its good bases is said to look like a **mix of two clones**, with its trace: pick a single colony and sequence it again. When the second peaks start at one place and carry on, it says where: two clones that differ by an insertion or deletion there.

- Turn on **Keep the reads and the result with this plasmid's files** to file the reads under **Files**, each noted with the date and what it showed. Checking changes nothing else; anyone who can open the plasmid can check reads, and keeping them needs the right to edit it.

- An AI assistant can do the same: upload the `.ab1` as a capture (or give it the read as text) and ask it to check the clone against the plasmid (see [AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants)).

### Tubes, boxes and files

- **Files**, on **Storage**, keeps what belongs with the plasmid: the sequencing reads (.ab1) that confirmed it, gel photos, the vendor's datasheet. Say in one line what they show. Pictures show a thumbnail; whoever added a file, or an admin, can take it off again. They come with your data in **Export my data**.

- Each tube keeps its miniprep's **Concentration** (ng/µL) and **260/280**, in the sheet and on its **Storage** tab, which also lists the notebook pages that link it.

### Sharing and bulk changes

- **Belongs to**: *Personal*, or *Lab common* — anyone can edit it (a shared stock plasmid), while only its owner or an admin changes whose it is or deletes it. The *Lab common* chip lists them.

- Select plasmids to set owner, resistance or Belongs to, move them to a box, or delete. Moved into another box with no position, a plasmid takes its next free cell. **Import from Excel** brings in your old list.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/plasmids

---

## Samples, orders, reagents, antibodies, viruses

Samples, orders, reagents, chemicals, antibodies, viruses, primers, glycerol stocks and cell lines.

### What this does for your week

Buying something and finding it again are the same chain, and it usually breaks where one person orders and another unpacks the box. BioManager keeps that chain in one place, so the shelf matches the record.

| Someone needs something | **New order** will not go out without item, vendor, catalogue number and quantity, which is what makes a reorder possible months later. |
|---|---|
| While it is coming | Requested → Ordered → Received, one tap each, on a table or a board you drag cards across. Everyone can see what is on its way instead of asking. |
| The box arrives | Mark it received and BioManager offers to put it on the shelf — [Receive an order into stock](https://biomanager.org/guide/receive-an-order) makes the reagent, antibody or virus record with the vendor, catalogue number and lot already filled in. |
| Months later | Expiring soon and Expired chips, and both on [Home](https://biomanager.org/guide/home-page). On anything running low, **Order again** opens a new order already filled in from the old one. |

What you stop doing: ordering a second one because nobody knew the first had arrived, retyping a catalogue number off a box, and finding the antibody expired the morning you needed it.

One engine, ten starting points, each with its own columns and statuses. Viruses, Primers and Glycerol stocks each name the plasmid they came from, so they sit with [Plasmids](https://biomanager.org/guide/plasmids) as tabs of one area, **Molecular biology** in the sidebar, rather than on their own:

| Samples | Tissue and material, linked to the animal it came from — pick the colony and type its ID in the **Source** cell, or tick a whole harvest and set it on all of them at once. Beside it, **Custom tag** shows that mouse's tag, straight from the colony, so re-tagging a mouse there updates every sample of it at once. If you hide **Custom tag** under **Columns** on the Mice tab, it goes from Samples too. Rest the pointer on the arrow after the ID for that mouse's sex, age, genotype, status, owner and cage, and the notebook pages that mention it, as the notebook shows over **@mouse**; click it to open the mouse in the colony. A tab for each type, each with its own columns ([Samples by type](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders#samples-by-type)): a tissue's *Tissue*, *Fixation* and *Orientation*; a DNA's or RNA's *Conc.* and its unit, *260/280*, *260/230* and *Volume (µL)*; and for every sample its *Genotype* and *Condition*. Stored at RT, 4 °C, −20 °C, −80 °C or LN₂ in a freezer box position. Available, in use, used up, discarded. |
|---|---|
| Orders | What the lab has asked for: vendor, catalogue number, quantity, price, grant account. Requested, ordered, received, cancelled — on a table or a **Board** you drag cards across. |
| Reagents | Quantity, concentration, CAS number, storage temperature, hazards, lot and expiry. In stock, low, empty, discarded. |
| Chemicals | The lab's chemical list, as you may keep it in Excel now: name, *Abbreviation*, *CAS*, *MW (g/mol)*, *Purity (%)*, and in the record *Formula* and *Density (g/mL)*; with quantity, lot, expiry, hazards and where each bottle is. *Hazard* takes several at once: flammable, toxic, corrosive and the rest, and the controlled classes a safety office asks about (drug precursor, explosive precursor, highly toxic, narcotic or psychotropic); **Configure** adds the lab's own. A **Formulation** in a [notebook page](https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook#data-and-calculators) picks chemicals from here by name, abbreviation or CAS number and works out the moles from what you weigh, and the [calculators](https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook#utilities) in Utilities know each molecular weight. In stock, low, empty, discarded. |
| Antibodies | Host, clonality, clone, conjugate, reactivity, applications, dilution, isotype, RRID, and where each vial is. |
| Viruses | AAV, lentivirus, rabies and other vectors: serotype, the plasmid it was made from (**Made from**), promoter, payload, titer, biosafety level, the date made, and each aliquot's place in a −80 °C box. The DNA icon beside the plasmid opens its sequence and map to read (editing stays on the plasmid's own page). In stock, low, used up, discarded. |
| Primers & oligos | Sequence (5′→3′), direction, target, its pair, stock µM and modification. *Length*, *GC %* and *Tm* are worked out from the sequence (nearest neighbour, 50 mM Na⁺, 250 nM). **Add primer pair** makes *name*-F and *name*-R at once, each naming the other, side by side in a box. A primer drawn on a plasmid's map comes here by itself, with the plasmid in its **Plasmid** column. Tick primers, then **Copy for ordering** or **Export for ordering** for the supplier. To order, ordered, in stock, low, used up, discarded. |
| Glycerol stocks | Bacteria carrying a plasmid, frozen in glycerol: the plasmid (**Plasmid**), strain, colony, resistance, how it was checked (digest, colony PCR, Sanger, whole plasmid), the date frozen, and its place in a −80 °C box. The plasmid's **Storage** tab lists its glycerol stocks and the box each is in. In stock, low, used up, discarded. |
| Cell lines | A frozen vial of each line or clone: species, parent, passage, freeze date, cells per vial, medium, selection, mycoplasma result and date, and its place in the LN₂ boxes. In stock, thawed, used up, discarded. |
| Custom list | Whatever you define. |

### Samples by type

Tissue blocks and tubes of DNA are kept differently and described differently, so Samples has a tab for each type above the sheet: **All**, then **tissue**, **blood**, **serum**, **DNA**, **RNA**, **protein** and the rest, each with how many it holds.

- **A tab shows only its own columns.** **tissue** has *Tissue* (the organ: lung, DRG…), *Fixation* (fresh frozen, 4% PFA, formalin, RNAlater…) and *Orientation* (sagittal, coronal…), and no 260/280; **DNA** and **RNA** have the concentration, its unit, 260/280, 260/230 and volume, and no fixation. **All** shows every column, with a dash where one isn't used for that sample's type.

- **The boxes follow the tab.** In **tissue**, **Box grid** and the box buttons show the boxes holding tissue, and the empty ones; a box still shows everything in it, so a cell another sample is in never looks free.

- **A new sample from a tab is of that type**, and its dialog asks only for that type's columns. Changing the **Type** in the dialog changes the fields it shows.

- **Genotype** comes from the source mouse: left empty, it shows that mouse's genotype from the colony, in grey, and follows it when the mouse is re-genotyped. Type one to give the sample its own. Search finds samples by either.

- **+** at the end of the tabs adds a type (slides, plasma, CSF…): anyone can, and it gets a tab of its own with the columns every type has. Renaming or removing a type is in **Configure**, under *Type choices*.

- Which columns a type has is each column's **Used for** in **Configure**: the types it is for, separated by commas, or empty for every type. Any inventory can have tabs: tick **A tab for each type** under *What it tracks*.

Brought your samples in from another database, with everything in the notes (*Tissue: Lung; Fixation: 4% PFA; control 6OHDA 2w*)? Tick them (**All** under the page size shows every row at once), then **Split notes** in the bar that appears. Each *Column: value* whose name is a column goes into it; the rest stays in the notes. A sample with no type that gets a column of one type only (a fixation) becomes that type. A column already holding something else is left as it is, and a name with no column is listed, so you can add it in Configure and split again. **Batch history** undoes it.

### Ordering, start to shelf

1. **New order.** Item, vendor, catalogue number and quantity are required (starred), so no order goes out half-filled. Type an item or catalogue number the lab has used before and pick it: the vendor, price and grant fill in from last time. The lab's admins are told of each new request.

2. **Follow it.** The status chips — *Requested, Ordered, Received, Cancelled* — show each stage in one tap; the person who requested it is notified as it moves.

3. **It arrives.** Mark it received and BioManager asks **Add it to stock?**: a new reagent, chemical, antibody or virus with its name, vendor, catalogue number, lot, quantity and expiry already filled in, opened for you to add where it's kept. (Later, the **To stock** button on the order does the same.) From then on the order shows *Reagents #8* and the reagent shows the order it came from; each opens the other.

4. **Running low?** On any reagent, chemical, antibody or virus, the cart button, **Order again**, opens a new order with its details and the quantity, price and grant of the last time it was ordered. While it is already on order the button says **On order**, and the new order opens with a note naming the open one and who asked for it.

### Low stock, from the quantity

Reagents, chemicals, antibodies, viruses and primers have a **Low at** column beside **Qty** and **Unit**, and the same field in the record's dialog under *Supply*. Write the quantity as a number (`12`, `2.5` or `2,5`) and set Low at in the same unit; from then on the status follows it:

- When the quantity falls to Low at or below, the status turns *low*; at 0, *empty* (*used up* in Viruses and Primers). Topped up above Low at, it is *in stock* again.

- Its owner is told when it runs low, once each time, in their own language (under *Orders* in Settings → Notifications; not for a change they made themselves). Low reagents, chemicals, antibodies and viruses are listed on Home's **Expiring & low stock** with what is left, and **Order again** starts the new order.

- A status chosen by hand stays as chosen. A quantity in words (*half a bottle*), a discarded item, or one with no Low at is left alone.

- In the sheet, a quantity or Low at is saved when you leave the cell or press Enter, so typing `12` doesn't pass through `1` on the way.

- Counted in ampoules, vials, tubes or bottles but used by the mL? Give the item a **Pack size**, what one of them holds (`10 mL`), in its dialog beside **Unit** (or show the column in the sheet; for many at once, tick them and use **Set field → Pack size**). An AI assistant told *2 mL used* then takes 0.2 of an ampoule off the quantity, and so does an experiment day recorded with **Take what they got off the inventory** ([Experiments](https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments#the-page)).

### Every inventory

- **Mine** and **Lab common** keep your own stock apart from the lab's shared shelf.

- *Expiring soon* (30 days) and *Expired* chips; expired and low stock also show on Home.

- **Box grid** places items in freezer boxes; the same boxes as everywhere else. A box's *Stored at* (−80 °C, LN₂…) goes to what is put in it, and moving the box moves theirs. In a box with no position given, an item takes the next free one. Marking a tube used up, empty or discarded frees its position; its location note keeps where it was. **New box** has **How many**, for a whole tower at once.

- **Kept in**, in a box's dialog, says which fridge, freezer or cabinet the box, shelf or drawer is in: *Fridge 2*, *Explosion-proof cabinet*. The **Box** column, labels and search then read *Fridge 2 › Box A · B3*, and the **Box grid** picks the fridge or cabinet first, then the box. Type a cabinet's name in the sheet's search to list everything in it, such as the solvents in the explosion-proof cabinet. A place typed once is offered again in every inventory.

- **Used in notebook pages**, at the bottom of a record's dialog, lists the pages that link it (`@antibodies 5`; see [Notebook](https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook)).

- **Renumber**, under **•••** (its creator, or an admin): each record's **#** is given when it is made, so after an import it follows the sheet's order. Renumber gives every record a new #, in the order of a column (B2 before B10), or as the number in its name (*B12* becomes #12, when every name has one, none twice and none missing; it names the records in the way). It lists each # now and new before anything changes. Links to them in the notebook (`@samples 12`) and orders put into stock follow; labels already printed keep the old #, but their QR code still opens the right record. **Settings → History** can undo it.

- **Configure** (its creator, or an admin): the name, what it tracks, the choices and statuses (renaming one relabels its items), your own columns, and which fields are **needed for a new item**.

- **A plasmid column** (the Viruses' **Made from**, or one you add in Configure as *A plasmid*): type the plasmid's number or name, or pick it from the list, and the cell opens that plasmid. The plasmid's **Storage** tab lists everything made from it, under *Made from this plasmid*.

*The reagents sheet*

*The orders board*

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders

---

## Receive an order into stock

When an order arrives, mark it received and add it to stock, with its details already filled in.

Who and where: Anyone who may edit the order · Desktop and lab server

1. Open Orders and find the order. The status chips, *Requested, Ordered, Received, Cancelled*, narrow the sheet to one stage.

2. Mark it received: set its **Status** to *received*, or on the **Board**, drag its card to the *Received* column.

3. BioManager asks **Add it to stock?** Under **Add to**, choose the reagents, chemicals, antibodies or viruses it goes into, and under **Belongs to**, whether it is lab common or yours. **Not now** leaves it; later, the **To stock** button on the order does the same.

4. Press **Add to stock**.

5. The new record opens with its name, vendor, catalogue number, lot, quantity and expiry already filled in from the order. Add where it is kept. If that database needs a field the order doesn't have, its form opens filled in from the order instead: fill in the rest and save.

From then on the order shows *Reagents #8* and the reagent shows the order it came from; each opens the other. The person who requested the order is notified as it moves. When it runs low, **Order again** (the cart button on the reagent, chemical, antibody or virus) opens a new order with its details.

*Add it to stock? — the new record is filled in from the order*

Related: [Samples, orders, reagents, antibodies, viruses](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders) [Notifications](https://biomanager.org/guide/notifications)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/receive-an-order

---

## Experiments, for every animal

Treatment groups, doses from body weight, readouts and the stats, for every animal.

### What this does for your week

An experiment is where a colony turns into data, and it is where records usually fall apart: doses on a paper sheet, weights in one person's phone, the groups remembered rather than written. This page keeps the regimen, the animals and the readout together, so the export is the experiment.

| Before it starts | Name it, set day 1 and the readout, and pull in the animals — a tank's fish or a cohort of mice — so the groups are written down before the first dose. |
|---|---|
| Each manipulation | **Record manipulation** writes what was just done to a whole group — Tamoxifen 20 mg/kg i.p. today — and doses are worked out from each animal's body weight rather than in your head. |
| At the bench | Scan the experiment's QR code with a phone for bench mode: one animal at a time, gloves on, recorded where you stand ([At the bench](https://biomanager.org/guide/phones-and-cage-cards)). |
| Afterwards | The chart shows the readout by group over the days. **Export** gives an Excel workbook — long for Prism or R, wide for a glance, with every animal's manipulations beside it. |

What you stop doing: transcribing a dosing sheet, recalculating mg/kg at the cage, and rebuilding the groups from memory when it is time to analyse.

Mice, zebrafish, flies, worms and your own organisms all have an **Experiments** tab beside their other tabs (Mice and Cages; Tanks and Fish; the vials or plates). **New experiment** there can start with a whole cage, tank, rack or housing of them. One page shows each experiment, and **All experiments** on it goes back to the tab.

| Mice | Mice, or a whole cage. Body weight (or tumour volume, a clinical score, survival). Injections, challenges, treatments, surgery, behaviour, stimulation, sampling, imaging. |
|---|---|
| Zebrafish | Fish rows, a whole tank, or a clutch's larvae. Survival (how many of those at the start are alive), standard length or a phenotype. Drug in the water, microinjection, heat shock, injury or fin clip. |
| Flies and worms | Vials or plates, or a whole rack; say how many each started with. They have no body weight: survival, or eclosion and climbing for flies, brood size and paralysis for worms. Drug in the food or on the plate, RNAi feeding, temperature shifts, starvation, infection, flipping to fresh food. |
| Any other organism | Animals, groups or cohorts, or a whole housing. Body weight, length, survival or a score. |

Any experiment can follow a readout of its own (**Readout → Something else…**): a number for each, or how many of those at the start.

### Readouts worked out from what you measure

Some readouts are a sum, not a reading: a tumour's volume from the calipers, fold change from a qPCR run. Choose one under **Readout → Worked out by BioManager from what you measure**, then type what you measured and let BioManager do the arithmetic, the same way every time. **New experiment** offers them too, with the **Control group** for ΔΔCt and fold change.

| Tumour volume (L × W² / 2) | Length and width in mm, the length the longer side. In mm³. |
|---|---|
| Tumour volume (π/6 × L × W × H) | Three diameters in mm, for a lab that measures the height too. Pick whichever your lab uses. |
| ΔCt | The Ct of the target gene and of the reference gene: target − reference. |
| ΔΔCt, Fold change (2^−ΔΔCt) | The same two Cts, against the mean ΔCt of the **Control group** (set beside the readout) on the same day. Enter the control animals' Cts first, or the whole day at once. |
| % of baseline | A value and its baseline, such as today's weight and day 1's. |
| Absorbance, blank subtracted | A well's OD and the blank's. |

- **Measure** (or **Record**) and **Another day** open the day with a box for each thing measured, for every animal; click a value in the sheet to change what it was worked out from. Point at a value to see what was measured, and **Export** has those beside each value.

- In **Bench mode** each animal gets a box for each measurement, and the value it worked out is shown as you go on.

- A number left out, below zero, a width longer than the length, a Ct of 60 or *Undetermined* is refused, saying why, rather than saved.

### Plates from a plate reader or qPCR machine

An ELISA, a viability assay or a qPCR run gives one number per well, and the work is knowing which well was which animal. Lay the plate out once, and each export goes straight into the readout.

1. **Plate layout**, above the sheet, opens the plate: 24, 48, 96 or 384 wells (**Wells**). Pick an animal on the left, or **Blank**, or **Standard** with its concentration, then click a well or drag across several; a row letter or column number takes the whole row or column, and **Empty** clears. **Fill in order** puts every animal not yet on the plate into the next empty wells, two or three each, across the rows or down the columns. Several wells for one animal are its replicates.

2. Give it a name and **Save layout**. It is kept with the experiment, and the next time the plate opens on the layout you last read onto (*Same as last plate*); change it, or start a **New layout**.

3. **Read a plate →**, then paste the export or choose its file (CSV, TSV or Excel). BioManager reads a grid with row letters A–H and column numbers 1–12 (several reads in one file, such as two wavelengths, can be chosen between), or a list of wells and values: Well and OD, or Well, Target and Ct (or Cq) from a qPCR run.

4. **Readout** says what the plate fills: the experiment's main readout, or another measure of the same animals kept beside it (below). **Another measure…** asks its name and its **Kind**: **A number**, with a unit, such as *IL-6 ELISA* in pg/mL, or one worked out from two genes' Cts, **ΔCt: target − reference**, **ΔΔCt, against a control group** or **Fold change (2^−ΔΔCt)** (the last two ask for the **Control group**), so a qPCR run can fill a gene's ΔCt beside a tumour volume. The next plate offers it by name, and asks for the genes again.

5. Each well's value shows on the plate, before anything is saved. A replicate far from the others (more than half a cycle for a Ct, a fifth of the value otherwise) is ringed in orange; a well past what the instrument reads (an OD over 10, a Ct over 50, *OVRFLW*) in red, and left out, as is *Undetermined*. Click any well to leave it out, and again to put it back.

6. Below the plate, each animal's wells, their mean and spread (CV), and the value it gets. Set the **Day**, then **Save readings**.

| A readout of your own, or another measure | (**Readout → Something else…** at the top, such as IL-6 in pg/mL, or **Another measure…** in the plate.) The mean of each animal's wells, less the blank's mean (**Take off the blank**). With standards of two or more concentrations, **Read each value off the standard curve** turns each into a concentration, and **Curve** chooses the curve: **Linear**, a straight line through the standards; **Log–log**, a straight line on log axes, for standards over several tenfold dilutions; or **4PL**, the four-parameter logistic, the S-shaped curve of an ELISA, for five or more concentrations. BioManager starts with 4PL when there are five or more standards spanning a tenfold dilution, and a straight line otherwise. The curve is drawn beside the plate, with the standards as dots and each animal as a square on it, and its equation and r² below. A value past the highest or lowest standard is marked; one past where a 4PL levels off can't be read at all, and says so (dilute the sample and read it again). A 4PL that doesn't fit the standards is refused, in words, rather than used. |
|---|---|
| Absorbance, blank subtracted | The mean OD less the blank's, kept with both. |
| ΔCt, ΔΔCt, fold change | Choose the **Target gene** and the **Reference gene** from the run (a housekeeping gene on it, such as Gapdh or Actb, starts as the reference); each animal's mean Ct of each is used, and ΔΔCt and fold change are against the **Control group** as when you type them. |

Saving a day that already has readings replaces them, and says so first. The plate is kept with the experiment: **Plates read**, under the layout, lists each with its day, layout, what it filled and its file. A saved plate is one step in **Batch history**: **Undo** there takes back all its readings and the plate together, and puts back any readings it replaced. Only the experiment's owner (or an admin) lays out and reads plates, as with the rest of the experiment.

#### Another measure beside the main readout

An experiment has one main readout: the one its plan, **Main readout day**, tests by day and bench mode are about. Something else measured on the same animals, such as an IL-6 ELISA at the end of a tumour experiment, is another measure, kept beside it rather than in its place. Each gets its own button on the sheet, next to the main readout's: the sheet shows its days (a cell can be typed or corrected there), and the chart below and its tests by day follow the button chosen. **Export** gives each measure a sheet of its own, and its tests under the main readout's in **Tests by day**. Changing the main readout keeps the other measures.

A measure worked out from Cts is typed in its cell as the two Cts, the target's then the reference's (*24.8 − 18.2*); a ΔCt measure also takes the ΔCt itself. Pointing at a cell shows the Cts it was worked out from, and its sheet in **Export** has them beside each value. ΔΔCt and fold change are against the control group's mean ΔCt on the same day, as for the main readout.

The **•••** beside the measure shown opens it: change its name or unit (its readings stay with it), its **Kind**, or the **Control group** of a ΔΔCt or fold change, or **Delete measure**. Another kind works its readings out again: a number keeps each value, ΔCt takes each from its two Cts, and ΔΔCt or fold change needs the two Cts of every reading (a number or a typed ΔCt has none, so it says so and changes nothing). Each change is one step in **Batch history**. Deleting asks first, saying how many readings go with it; it is one step in **Batch history**, whose **Undo** brings back the measure and its readings together.

### The page

- **The experiment** on top: name, status, start (day 1), end, readout and description, saved as you type.

- **The sheet of its animals** switches between **Treatment** — each manipulation day a column: ✓ and the amount for each animal that got it (click to change) — and the readout, a column a day, typed in place (**Another day** adds one). Each animal's group is edited here too.

- **Record manipulation** records what was just done — *the HDM group got Tamoxifen 20 mg/kg i.p. today* — or a day of the regimen. For a dose per body weight it works out each animal's amount from its latest weight, and the volume given the solution (*10 mg/mL*). Tick the animals it was done to and, if you want, **make a sample record for each one** in Samples, with the animal as its source.

- Each day recorded keeps the **Reagent used** and its **Lot**, and the expiry the lot had. It starts as the item picked in the regimen; when the regimen names only what is given (*Tamoxifen*), the one item of that name in your inventories is picked, and kept on the regimen for next time (with several, they come first in the list: pick the bottle you used). A new bottle is another item, or type its lot. A lot already past its expiry on the day is recorded, with a warning. Tick **Take what they got off the inventory** to take the amounts (or volumes) the animals got off the item's quantity, turned into its unit (a **Pack size** turns mL into ampoules); it is taken once, however often the day is saved, and **Undo: not done** puts it back. The lot shows on the day in the list and the sheet, in **Export**, and in the experiment's notebook block.

- **The chart** shows the readout by group over the days (the value, or its % of the first; for a count, % of those at the start). Each manipulation day is a dashed line: point at it to see what was done that day, by whom. Stars mark the days the groups differ, and **Tests by day** below lists each test (Welch's t-test for two groups, one-way ANOVA for more, χ² for counts), each day on its own.

### The regimen

**Regimen** lists what is to be done and on which days: the kind, what, dose, route, solution, group and days (`1`, `2-5`, `2/3/4/5`, `1, 8, 15`). Day 1 is the start date. A **Stimulation** (optogenetic, electrical, TMS…) also has its **Frequency**, **Intensity**, **Pulse width** and **Duration**, as you write them: *20 Hz*, *5 mW*, *5 ms*, *30 min*. The days to do are on the calendar, and the experiment's owner gets a notification each morning of what is due (turn it off in **Settings → Notifications → Experiments**). Nothing is done until someone records it on the page. **Save as a regimen…** keeps it to plan the next cohort from.

### Animals that may need a look

Home's card [Animals that may need a look](https://biomanager.org/guide/home-page#animals) reads a mouse experiment's records too. It says what they show, never a diagnosis:

- **Losing weight**: a mouse whose latest weight is the lab's percentage (15% unless an admin sets another in **Settings → General → Weight loss to flag**) or more below its first weight in an experiment that has started, or below its heaviest of the last 30 days.

- **Not weighed in their experiment**: in an active experiment whose readout is body weight, an animal (a mouse, or any other organism weighed in the experiment) not weighed for longer than the longest gap between the regimen's weighing days (a *Readout day* on days 1, 4, 7: 3 days), or 7 days when it plans none or its last has passed. Animals left out of the analysis aren't counted.

- **Status and experiment disagree**: a mouse whose status is *experiment* while it is in no planned, active or paused experiment, or *geno*, *breeder* or *transfer* while it is in an active one.

### Planned experiments, and changes from the plan

An AI assistant can design an experiment with you: the groups, the regimen from your saved regimens, how many animals each group needs, and which animals the lab has for it ([AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#plan)). It arrives as **Planned**, and nothing of it is due yet: not on Home, the calendar or in notifications.

1. Check the groups and their animals, the regimen, the **Main readout day** and the **Planned test** (Welch's t-test, one-way ANOVA or χ²). Change anything; while it is planned, nothing asks why.

2. Press **Start**. Day 1 is today, unless you set a start date. BioManager keeps a copy of the plan.

From then on, four changes ask for a one-line reason, because each can change what the result means: the main readout or its day; the groups (adding, taking out or moving animals, renaming or merging a group); leaving an animal out of the analysis; and the test. **Why the change from the plan?** takes the reason, and **Save with this reason** saves both; **Cancel** leaves it as it was. Nothing is ever refused, and dates, notes and extra readouts never ask.

- **Leave out…** on an animal's row keeps its readout in the sheet but leaves it out of the chart and the tests by day, with the reason; **Put back** counts it again.

- **Changes from the plan** lists each change: what, before → after, the reason, who and when. Below it, **Planned → done** sets the plan beside what happened.

- The Excel export gets a *Plan and deviations* sheet, so a paper's methods can say what was set in advance and what changed.

- Experiments started before this, and those made without a plan, never ask.

### At the bench, and afterwards

- **Bench mode** (scan its QR code with a phone): pick what you are doing — the main readout, another measure of the experiment, or a manipulation due — then one animal at a time with big numbers: type each weight, count or value, or give each today's manipulation and tap **Given ✓**; record it at the end, with the **Reagent used** and its **Lot** filled in as on the page. **Scan a card** reads a cage, tank or vial card with the phone's camera and jumps to the animal in it.

- **Export** downloads an Excel workbook: the readout, long (for Prism or R) and wide, each animal's manipulations with the reagent and lot it got, the tests by day, and a sheet for each other measure.

- **Add to notebook** makes your notebook page for the experiment, with a live view of its manipulations and readout (`/experiment` adds one to any page; **Freeze a copy** keeps it as it is now).

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments

---

## Notebook and utilities

Notebook pages, paper notes, protocols, data sheets, signing, and the bench calculators.

### Pages

- Pages in **Topics**, written like a document and kept as Markdown. Topics are folders, listed in the notebook's sidebar: **+** beside *Topics* names a new one, a topic's own **+** starts a page in it, and its **•••** renames it or deletes it with its pages. Drag a page onto a topic to move it there. The sidebar's button at the top (or `Ctrl`+`\`, `⌘`+`\` on a Mac) hides it, so the page has the window; the same button beside the page's place brings it back.

- **New page** asks four things, each labelled: the **Title**, the **Topic** it goes in, its **Kind**, and what to **Start from**. Each kind says what it adds:

- **Note**: just the page.

- **Experiment**: a status, the times it started and finished, and the protocol it follows.

- **Protocol**: numbered versions, **Run** step by step, and experiments started from it.

- **Reading**: a paper, with its authors, DOI, Zotero link and a cover, listed in **Reading** (below).

- **Meeting**: a presenter rotation, and tasks naming `@someone` sent to their calendar.

- **Seminar**: the speaker and their affiliation, listed in **Reading** beside the papers.

- **Daily log** is *Today*, one page a day.

**Start from** lists the built-in starters of that kind (an Experiment can start as *Cloning*, *Western blot* or *qPCR*), an empty page, and your templates of that kind. **Import .md** at the bottom brings in a Markdown file instead. Type **/** at the start of a line for a menu of blocks: tables, plots, protocols, calculators and the rest below.

- **Templates**: ⋯ → **Save as template** asks for a name and **Who can use it** (just you, everyone in the lab, or a project group); a name you already use asks before replacing that template. It keeps the page's kind (an Experiment template makes Experiments) and is listed under **Start from** for that kind. **Structure only** keeps the headings, steps and table headers and leaves out the results, ticks, readings, pictures and what was written under Results, Observations or Conclusion.

- In the row at the top of the window, the page's place reads like a file path: its topic, then the pages it sits in. Click the topic to move the page: search your topics, or type a new name to make one. The pages inside it move with it. Above the title is the page's kind: click it to change it, which never moves the page. Hover there for **Add cover**, a picture across the top of the page (uploaded, or one of the page's own pictures); **Change cover** and **Remove** are on the cover. The title wraps onto as many lines as it needs. Under it are its date, status and tags; once other pages link to it, **Linked from** lists them.

- Write as in Notion: type **/** and a few letters of what you want (`/h2`, `/toggle`; Chinese words work too, `/分栏`).

- **Heading 1–3**, **Bulleted list**, **Numbered list**, **Checklist**, **Quote** and **Divider**.

- **Callout**: a coloured box for what nobody should miss. Its icon picks the kind: note, tip, important, warning or caution. **Warning** starts as one.

- **Toggle**: a line that opens to show what it hides, such as raw counts or the long version of a method. Click the arrow to open or close it. That choice is yours alone and doesn't open it for anyone else.

- **2 columns** or **3 columns**: a gel picture beside its notes. Inside them, the bar above the toolbar adds a column, removes one, or puts them back one under the other. On a phone they stack.

- **Colour and highlight** (also the **A** on the toolbar): colours the selected text, or the whole line when nothing is selected. Typing `==text==` highlights it in yellow.

- **Page**: a new page inside this one, in the same topic, opened in a BioManager tab to write in. In the sidebar it sits under this page; the arrow beside a page shows or hides the pages in it. **Link to page**, or typing `[[`, finds a page that exists, or makes a new one named as you typed. **Turn into page** makes the line a new page with its words as the title. A link to a page shows that page's title as it is now. Clicking it, or any link to a page of the app, opens it in a BioManager tab; links to the web open in your browser.

- **Table of contents**: the page's headings, kept up to date, each one a link.

- **Date…** inserts a day you pick. **Reminder** adds a to-do to your calendar on the day and time you choose, and writes a link to it in the page (⏰ and the date).

The formatting bar floats at the bottom of the window, in one row:

- the text's style (text, headings, quote, code block) and lists;

- bold, italic, strikethrough, colour and link;

- **Picture or file**, the timer, **Insert**, undo, redo and **Run**.

On a narrow screen it scrolls sideways. All of it stays readable Markdown: a callout is GitHub's `> [!WARNING]`, a toggle is `<details>`, and columns are Pandoc's `::: column`, so an exported page reads anywhere.

- Type `@` to link a mouse, plasmid, order or any inventory record — an antibody, a sample, a primer (`@antibodies 5`), found by its name, catalogue number or lot (a lot or catalogue number typed in full, like `@0012`, comes first; names such as *anti-β-actin* or *Waf1/Cip1* are found as written), a database by its name (`@antib` offers *Antibodies*, and picking it lists its records), or a colleague (`@jordan`). A colleague is shown in their colour, and hovering the name shows who they are: name, what they do, admin, member or guest, email, project groups, and how long they've been in the lab. They're told they were mentioned, and an action item names them. The page and a record then point at each other, and the record lists the page under **Used in notebook pages**. The chip shows the record's name after its number (*@antibodies 5 · anti-p53*). Hover over one for its details; clicking it opens the record, and **↗** (or `⌘`/`Ctrl`-click) opens it in a new BioManager tab.

- **Daily log** (*Today*) and **Meetings**: **Meetings** in the sidebar lists each meeting series, where you edit its day, place and presenting order. A presenter rotation, shared meeting notes, and action items (`- [ ] @name …, due …`) sent to that person's to-dos — from any page, with ⋯ → **Send @name tasks as to-dos**.

- An AI assistant you connected can add lines to the **Log** of today's daily log, once you approve them ([AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants)). If the page is open, the line appears in it within a few seconds.

### Paper notes and Reading

- A **Reading** page (start one with **Paper notes**) keeps the paper's **Authors**, **Journal**, **Year**, **DOI**, **Link** and **Zotero** link as rows under its title; click a row to type in it. The ↗ beside the DOI, the link or the Zotero link opens it; the Zotero one opens the item in Zotero on your computer.

- **Fill in**: paste a DOI, a doi.org link, or the item copied from Zotero and press `Enter`, and the rows and an empty title are filled in. In Zotero, set **Settings → Export → Item Format** (Quick Copy) to BibTeX, RIS or CSL JSON, select the paper and press `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`C` (`⌘`+`Shift`+`C` on a Mac). CSL JSON also brings the Zotero link. A DOI on its own is looked up at Crossref, which needs the internet; pasting from Zotero doesn't. **Paper** in New page does the same before the page is made, and names the page after the paper.

- Give a paper notes a **cover**: its key figure, uploaded or picked from the pictures in the page.

- **Reading** in the notebook's sidebar lists every paper and talk you can open, yours and those shared with you, as cards with their covers. **Papers** and **Talks** narrow it, and the picture button shows every picture in them instead, so you can find a paper by a figure you remember; click one to open its page. The search reads titles, authors, journals, DOIs, tags and the captions of pictures. The notebook's own search finds a paper by its authors and DOI too.

- **Paper notes from Zotero**: each paper you add to Zotero can become a paper note by itself. On zotero.org, open **Settings → Security → Create new private key**, tick **Allow library access** (and read access to groups, for a lab group library), and save. In BioManager, **Zotero** on the Reading page: paste the key, **Connect**, then pick the **Library**, a **Collection** (a collection called *BioManager*, say, so only the papers you put there get notes) and the **Topic** the notes go in. From then on, a paper added there becomes a note the next time you open the notebook, with its details, abstract and tags filled in; **Check now** looks at once. **Also the papers already there** makes notes for those too. A paper gets one note, ever, even if you change it in Zotero or delete its note. Zotero has to sync to zotero.org, and the computer or server running BioManager has to reach it. **Disconnect** forgets the key and keeps the notes.

### Experiments and protocols

- **Experiments**: aim, setup, samples and lot numbers, steps, results and a summary. **Start experiment**, beside the status, and **Finished** stamp the times; running experiments are listed at the top of the sidebar. (The colony's **Experiments** tab groups the animals.)

- **Colony experiment** (`/experiment`) shows an experiment on any of your animals in the page: each day's manipulation, the reagent and lot it used (*(expired)* when the lot was past its expiry that day), when it was done and by whom, the amount each mouse got, and the body weights as a table and a chart (grams or % of the first weight, with the manipulation days marked). When the experiment has other measures beside its main readout (an ELISA a plate filled), a button for each switches the table and chart to it, and the page keeps the one you picked. It stays up to date; **Freeze a copy** keeps what it shows now in the page, so later changes to the experiment don't alter your record. On the experiment itself, **Add to notebook** makes your page for it with this block already in.

- **Protocols** with numbered versions. **Start experiment**, in the protocol's bar, copies the steps as a checklist and records the version; **Run mode** takes you through it at the bench, one step at a time.

- **Protocols** in the sidebar opens the lab's protocols as a page: search them, open one to read or change it, or make one with **New protocol**. Sort them into folders: **New folder**, then drag a protocol onto it, or pick its folder with the folder button on its card or in the protocol's own bar. Pick a folder's icon when you make it, and change its name or icon with **Edit folder** inside it. Folders are shared with the whole lab; you file the protocols you can edit. Below are a dozen common protocols built in: open one to read it, and **Copy** it to make your own. In a page, `/protocol` lists the same protocols beside it, folder by folder, to insert one.

### Data and calculators

- **Data sheets**: paste from Excel or a CSV, add formula columns, and get a plot (bar, dot, box, scatter, line) with error bars, a fitted line and a t-test, Mann–Whitney or ANOVA. Paste a log with its headers (time down the first column, readings such as temperature and pressure beside it) and it is drawn as a line over time; **Y** picks the reading. **Plate reader** and **qPCR** blocks read concentrations off a standard curve and ΔΔCt fold changes.

- **Formulation** (`/formulation`): what goes into a reaction or a batch, by mass. In **Component**, type a chemical's name, abbreviation or CAS number and pick it from the lab's [Chemicals](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders) database: its molecular weight, purity, density and lot come with it, and the chemical's **Used in notebook pages** lists the page. Type the **Mass** you weigh and **Amount** gives the moles. Mark one row as the basis (the round button beside **Equiv.**) and give the others in equivalents: the mass to weigh follows, and changes when the basis does. Each row shows its **wt %**, a liquid its volume, and the total is underneath.

- **Buffer recipes** scale with the volume; common buffers are built in and the lab's own are shared. **Recipes** in the sidebar opens them: open one to change it, make one with **New recipe**, sort them into folders as protocols are, or **Save a copy** of a built-in one. **Load from library** in a recipe block lists them by folder. **Calculators** for dilution, molarity, master mix, serial dilution, ligation, cells, gels, DNA/RNA and **Protein (A₂₈₀)**: paste the sequence (or give ε and MW) and the reading, and it gives µM and mg/mL. Durations in a step get a **⏱** timer, named from the step's own words; time points (*6, 24, 48 h*, *at 24 h*, *the 48 h samples*) don't. Times on a page (*started 16:00*) are on the lab's clock, whatever your computer's time zone.

### Signing a page

When a page should be the record of your work, **Sign** it — your choice, page by page; nothing asks you to. You confirm who you are (your password, or your user name if you sign in with Google or Microsoft) and what signing means. Its exact text is fingerprinted and kept as a version, any live experiment in it is frozen as it is then, and the page is locked: nobody can change or delete it. A lab mate can **Witness** it. To change it, its owner **Amends** it with a reason; the reason and every signature stay with the page, each showing whether the page still reads as it did when signed.

### Working together

Share a page to read or edit, with people, everyone in the lab or a [project group](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups); editors type in it at the same time. A page's pictures and files go with it: only the people who can open the page can open them. Comments on a passage, with `@name` telling that person (switch these notices off under **Settings → Notifications**). **Version history** keeps every editing session to compare or restore. **Share**, **Comments**, **Sign** and **History** are in the row at the top of the page; each opens on the right, and the list of pages folds away while it is open. **Tags and search** work across every page you can open.

### Utilities

**Utilities**, under Notebook in the sidebar, holds the bench calculators and reference tables. Type in the search at the top what you are doing, in the bench's words: *c1v1*, *nanodrop*, *× g*, *MOI*, *稀释*; a typo or a plural still finds it, and a chemical's name (*MgCl2*) opens **Make a solution** with it filled in. Or open one from its group. **Pin** a tool to keep it at the top; the ones you opened last are under **Recent**.

A tool opens on a worked example, with the answer beside what you type, and changes as you type. Where a tool can work out more than one thing, **Work out** says which (the stock volume, or the final concentration); tools that do related jobs have modes along the top. Each remembers what you last typed on this computer, **Reset** goes back to the example, and **Copy** takes the answer, tables too, to paste into a notebook page or a sheet.

- **Solutions**: **Make a solution**: what to weigh for a molarity, a percent, from a concentrated liquid (37 % HCl, glacial acetic acid, 50 % NaOH) or in another hydrate or salt; **Dilute (C₁V₁)**, which also goes between mg/mL and µM when you give the MW, and takes × stocks; **Serial dilution**, by a round transfer (10 µL into 90 µL) or a fold per step; **Buffer at a pH**: what to weigh and how much concentrated acid or base to titrate with, or the two phosphate salts, at the temperature you use it. Type a chemical's name or formula to fill its molecular weight (*MgCl2·6H2O* and *magnesium chloride hexahydrate* are the same one). The lab's own come first: its [Chemicals](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders) database, by name or abbreviation. One it doesn't know leaves the weight for you to type.

- **DNA & cloning**: DNA / RNA concentration and purity from A₂₆₀; ng ↔ pmol ↔ copies (and ng/µL to nM); primer Tm, the annealing temperature and extension time for Taq or Q5/Phusion, and the water to resuspend; a restriction digest; ligation, with the whole reaction; HiFi/Gibson assembly; agarose gels.

- **PCR & qPCR**: Master mixes; ΔΔCt from a pasted table of Ct values (sample, gene, Ct; replicates averaged, fold change ± SD) or from four numbers; qPCR efficiency from a standard curve; equal RNA or DNA input for an RT.

- **Protein**: Concentration from A₂₈₀, with ε and MW from the sequence (cysteines paired or reduced); a BCA, Bradford or ELISA curve read off for your samples, replicates averaged; equal loading for a gel; SDS-PAGE recipes; concentrating and dialysis.

- **Cell culture**: Counting cells; seeding plates; splitting so a flask is ready on the day, and doubling time; drug and vehicle, one dose or a dose series that keeps the DMSO the same in every well; transfection, scaled or for lentivirus packaging; virus for an MOI, and the titer from a dilution series; freezing down; antibiotics for selection.

- **Bacteria & yeast**: OD₆₀₀ to cells, diluting back, and the time to an OD; antibiotics for media, and LB, agar and antibiotic to pour plates.

- **Bench & animals**: rpm ↔ × g, from one of **the lab's rotors** (anyone in the lab adds them once, with the radius and top speed); a **dosing sheet** that turns a list of animals and weights into µL each and the solution to make; sample size per group.

**The lab's own**: a calculation your lab does that isn't here becomes a tool of its own. **Make a tool** on that card, give it a name, its inputs (a short name to use in formulas, a label, a unit and an example value) and its answers, each a formula over those names: *culture * want / (stock - want)*. A formula takes numbers, + − * / ^, brackets, *pi* and sqrt, ln, log10, log2, exp, abs, round, min, max and pow; an answer given a name can be used by the answers after it. The preview works it out as you type and marks a formula it can't read. Everyone in the lab finds it in the search and the card; the person who made it, or an admin, can **Edit** or delete it. Units are labels, so keep the numbers in the units you name.

**Reference** tables: plates and flasks, buffer pKa, stocks and antibiotics (what each is dissolved in and how it keeps), agarose % by size, DNA ladders, concentrated reagents and molecular weights. A link to a tool (`…/utilities#dilute`) opens it.

*Utilities*

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook

---

## Sign a notebook page

When a page should be the record of your work, sign it: its text is fingerprinted and the page is locked.

Who and where: Whoever may edit the page · Desktop and lab server

1. Open the page in the Notebook.

2. Press **Sign** at the top of the page. The page's owner, and anyone it is shared with to edit, can sign it; anyone else can witness it once it is signed.

3. Under **What you are saying**, choose whether you did this work or reviewed the page.

4. Confirm who you are: **Your password**, or, if you sign in with Google or Microsoft, your user name.

5. Press **Sign and lock**.

Its exact text is fingerprinted and kept as a version, any live experiment in it is frozen as it is then, and the page is locked: nobody can change or delete it. The button now says **Signed**; it lists every signature, each showing whether the page still reads as it did when signed. A lab mate can open it and **Witness** the page.

> **Changing a signed page** Its owner presses **Signed**, writes **Why it is being amended** and presses **Open to amend**. The reason and every signature stay with the page; sign it again when it is done.

*Signing a page: what you are saying, your password, and Sign and lock*

Related: [Signing a page](https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook#signing) [Notebook and utilities](https://biomanager.org/guide/notebook)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/sign-a-notebook-page

---

## Calendar

Experiments, to-dos and bookings, with the colony's dates filled in for you.

- **Month, Week, Day** and **List** views. Filled in for you: weanings, genotyping and sac reminders, fly and worm flips and egg collections, organism schedules, zebrafish tanks and reagent expiry. Clicking one (once, in every view) opens the record it came from. A link can open a given view and day: `/calendar?view=week&date=2026-10-05`.

- The month (or week, or day) is the page's title. Back, **Today** and Forward, the **Month** / **Week** / **Day** / **List** switch and **New event** are in the row at the top.

- Beside the grid are a small month to jump around, a **Show** list with a colour and a count for each kind (events, to-dos, the colony, stocks and organisms, supplies, protocols, equipment, time away, connected calendars), the instruments and the protocols under way.

- **New event** offers an event, a to-do (due today, tomorrow, next week, or a date), **Book equipment**, **Time away** and **Start a protocol**. Drag an event, to-do or booking to move it.

- **Who sees it**, for an event or a to-do: *Only me*, *Everyone in the lab* or one of your [project groups](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups). Your own is seen by nobody else, admins included. A shared event is changed only by whoever added it and admins; a shared to-do anyone it is for can tick off. A new event starts as the lab's, a new to-do as yours.

- **Repeats**: an event every N days, weeks or months, or every month on the same weekday (*the first Monday*), until a date. **Delete this one** takes out a single date and **Change this one only** moves or changes it alone; Save changes every repeat.

- **Protocols**: write the steps once in days from day 0 (tamoxifen days 0–4, implant day 14, perfuse day 42), then start it for an experiment or a cohort. Every step lands on its day; move day 0 and they all move. A run keeps the steps it started with if the protocol is edited later. (These put the days on the calendar; the notebook's protocols hold the bench steps.)

- **Equipment**: add the lab's instruments under **Manage**, and **Edit** one there to rename it, say where it is or change its colour; its bookings follow. A booking that overlaps another is refused, saying who has it and when. A new booking can repeat every day, weekday or week until a date — each repeat is a booking of its own, and if one clashes none is made. **Duplicate**, on an open booking, books the same instrument and times on another day.

- **Time away**: leave or a conference. **Away soon** lists what of theirs falls due meanwhile — animals, vials, to-dos, bookings, protocol steps — and asks who covers it; that person is told.

- **Connected calendars** shows Google Calendar and any iCal subscription alongside, read-only.

- **On your phone**: a private link (just your things, or the whole lab's) for Apple, Google or Outlook Calendar. It updates about every hour. **Make a new link** stops the old one working.

*The calendar*

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/calendar

---

## Book equipment

Book time on a shared instrument in the calendar, so two people never turn up for the confocal at once.

Who and where: Anyone in the lab · Desktop and lab server

1. Open the Calendar. If the instrument isn't listed under **Equipment** in its sidebar, press **Manage** there, give its **Name** and **Where**, and press **Add instrument**. **Edit** one there to rename it, say where it is or change its colour; its bookings follow.

2. Press the arrow beside **New event** and choose **Book equipment**. Or press **New event** and choose **Booking**.

3. Pick the **Instrument**, the **From** and **To** times, and say **What for**.

4. To book it again and again, choose **Every day**, **Every weekday** or **Every week**, and the date it runs **until**. Each repeat is a booking of its own.

5. Press **Save**.

The booking is on the calendar; drag it to move it. A booking that overlaps another is refused, saying who has it and when, and if one repeat clashes, none is made. **Duplicate**, on an open booking, books the same instrument and times on another day.

*Book equipment: the instrument, the times, and what for*

Related: [Calendar](https://biomanager.org/guide/calendar) [Home](https://biomanager.org/guide/home-page)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/book-equipment

---

## Who can do what

Who can see and change what in a lab: members, owners and admins.

### The roles

Everyone in a lab has one role. A role never takes away what you own: it adds what else you may touch.

| Member | Changes their own records, and the lab's shared ones. Most people in a lab are members. |
|---|---|
| Animal care | Technicians and vets: may change *any* lab member's animals, cages, tanks and vials — weights, moves, flips, health. Other people's experiments, notebook pages and settings stay theirs. Their own records they keep like a member. |
| Facility manager | Animal care, plus the facility itself: racks, rooms, incubators, water systems and each database's settings. Not accounts. |
| Admin | Everything, including accounts, roles and [Lab setup](https://biomanager.org/guide/lab-setup), and the audit log. A lab needs at least one. |
| [Guest](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests) | Someone outside the lab, on a pass that ends by itself after a day, three days, a week or 30 days. They see only what the pass opens, and can never keep a copy of the lab. |

An admin changes a role from the **···** beside someone in **Settings → People & access**, and cannot change their own — so a lab can never lock its last admin out.

### Which rule wins

You may change a record if *any one* of these is true: you own it; it is shared with the lab or with a [project group](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups) you are in; or your role covers it. Nothing takes a permission away again, so you never have to work out which rule lost.

### What is yours

- **You edit what you own** — your mice, cages, vials, plasmids and items.

- **Shared cages and anything marked lab common** belong to the whole lab. A cage whose purpose is *Breeder* starts out *Shared*; any other cage (an experiment cage, a *Breeding* one) starts *Personal*. Only its owner or an admin shares a cage, makes it personal or gives it to someone else; admins and animal care can still see and change every cage.

- **Giving something away is its owner's call**, in every database. You may edit a shared breeding tank, a lab stock vial or a lab-common plasmid, but only its owner or an admin changes its **Owner** or whom it is shared with (animal care may too, for the animals, cages, tanks and vials they look after). A new owner is always someone in the lab: pick them from the list.

- **Everyone sees the lab's databases**, because a census with holes is not a census.

- **Personal databases** (*Just you* on their tile) are seen only by their owner and admins; a [project group's](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups) by its members and admins.

- **Admins** can change anything, change the lab's setup in Settings, approve people, and read the audit log.

- **Animal care** (technicians, vets; a role set in **Settings → People & access**) may change any lab's animals, cages, tanks and vials, but not other people's experiments, notebook pages or settings (their own they keep like a member). A **Facility manager** also runs the racks, rooms, incubators, water systems and each database's settings, but not accounts.

- **Racks & boxes** in **Settings → Statistics** (admins) says who may resize, rename or delete each rack, box and incubator, in every database — fish racks and the racks of your own databases too. One with nobody is for admins only.

When a record isn't yours, BioManager says whose it is instead of just refusing.

### When someone leaves the lab

Their records do not disappear — mice, cages, plasmids and pages stay exactly where they are, still in their name, so the colony and the notebook stay whole. To hand the work on:

1. On each sheet, select their records and use **Set field → Owner** to put them in the new person's name. ([Many at once](https://biomanager.org/guide/many-at-once) does a whole sheet in one go.)

2. An admin sets their role, in **Settings → People & access**, to whatever is right now they have gone.

3. A guest pass needs nothing: it ends on its own date.

A notebook page they signed stays signed in their name — that is the point of signing, and nobody can change it afterwards, including an admin.

### Troubleshooting

#### I can't edit a record

It belongs to someone else and isn't shared: BioManager says whose it is. Ask them, or an admin.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/who-can-do-what

---

## Project groups

Share animals, stock, databases and pages among the people on a project.

Who and where: Since 1.0.3

A group is some of the lab working on one project: a layer between you and the whole lab. **Settings → People & access → Project groups** lists them; open one to see who is in it and what they may do. An admin makes a group and names it; an admin or the group's *leads* add and remove people. Someone can be in several groups.

Each person in a group is a **Lead** (runs the group: adds and removes people and sets what it may do), a **Member** (does what the group's switches allow) or **Can only view** (sees what is shared with the group and changes nothing, for a rotation student or a collaborator). Only an admin makes someone a lead. Under **In this group, members may**, a lead or an admin chooses:

- **Edit the group's animals and stock** (on to start);

- **Add and change records in the group's databases** (on); off, they can look but not change anything there;

- **Edit each other's records there** (off): off, each person edits only what they added;

- **Edit notebook pages shared with the group** (on): off, a page shared with the group to edit opens to read;

- **Tick off the group's to-dos** (on);

- **Share their own things with the group** (on): off, only its leads share with it.

Each starts as groups have always worked, so nothing changes until someone changes it. Leads and admins may always do all of them; the owner of a record may always edit it.

- **Shared with a group.** Wherever you choose *Shared* or *Lab common*, your groups are offered as well: a breeder cage, a plasmid or a reagent shared with a group is its members' to edit, as the group allows. For a breeding tank or a lab stock vial, pick the group under **Shared with** in its dialog. Everyone in the lab still sees them.

- **A group's database.** When you make a database, **Who is it for?** offers your groups: only their members (and admins) see it, and they are told it was added. **Share with the group** on the Databases page gives one of your own to a group.

- **A group's events and to-dos.** On the calendar, **Who sees it** offers your groups: the group's members see it on their calendar (and a to-do on Home), and any of them can tick a to-do off; only its maker or an admin changes an event or deletes a to-do.

- **Notebook.** **Share** on a page offers your groups as well as people, to view or to edit; a template can be for a group (**Who can use it**).

- **The colony.** **My groups**, beside My colony, shows the mice and cages of everyone in your groups.

Deleting a group (admins) makes what was shared with it its owner's own again (a breeding tank or a stock vial the lab's, as its purpose says), and a group's databases their maker's.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups

---

## People and guests

Approve sign-ups, manage admins and accounts, offer Google, Microsoft or institution sign-in, and let guests in.

Who and where: Admins

- **Where**: **Settings → People & access**. Everyone sees the lab's people there; admins change them, from the **···** beside each person.

- **Joining**: New sign-ups wait under **Waiting to join** until an admin presses **Approve**. Members can also sign in with Google or Microsoft, or with the institution's own account, if the server offers it, and connect it under **Settings → Sign-in & security** ([setting it up](https://biomanager.org/server#sign-in)).

- **Admins**: The **···** beside someone sets their role (admin, member, animal care, facility manager), resets their password, or disables the account. Keep at least two admins.

- **Leaving**: **Settings → Statistics** shows how many animals each person keeps; hand their racks over there (who may change each rack), give their records to someone else with **Set field → Owner**, then disable the account. Their records and history stay.

- **Guests**: For someone outside the lab — a collaborator, a visitor — for a day to a month: **New guest pass** under **Guests** (admins), who it's for and how long, **Make a code**. They open the link, enter the code, and work as a member with their own account until the pass ends or you press **End now**. On a Tailscale server, the admin can let guests in from the internet without Tailscale ([how](https://biomanager.org/server#guests)). Someone without a code chooses **No code? Ask the lab's admins for one** on the guest page, and every admin gets it as a notification, with how to reach them; **Forgot your password?** on the sign-in page asks the same way.

### Troubleshooting

#### I forgot my password

Ask an admin: the **···** beside you in **Settings → People & access** resets it.

#### My new account is waiting for an admin to approve it

The first account made in a lab becomes its admin, and every account after that waits until an admin approves it in **Settings → People & access**. On the desktop app, that means an account was made on this computer before yours, perhaps by you when you first opened it: sign in with that one, and approve the new one if you want both.

#### Nobody can sign in to the lab on my computer

On the desktop app, **Start a new lab** at the bottom of the sign-in page sets this computer's lab aside and starts an empty one, whose first account is its admin. Nothing is deleted: the old lab, with its accounts, records and files, is kept in the data folder under `old-labs`, and **Bring back a lab set aside** (on the sign-in, a new lab's first page, or **Settings → Lab**) brings it back. Press **Set this lab aside**, then **Close BioManager** and open it again. A lab server has no such button: whoever runs it can reset an admin's password there, or start the lab over ([its runbook](https://biomanager.org/server#after)).

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests

---

## Invite someone to the lab

Bring a new member onto your lab server: they make their own account, and an admin lets them in.

Who and where: Admins · Lab server

1. Send them your lab server's address.

2. They open it, press **Ask to join** and fill it in. Every admin is told at once, and their page changes as soon as one approves them; they can't sign in before that. If the server offers it, they can also sign in with Google or Microsoft, or with the institution's own account, and connect it under **Settings → Sign-in & security**, in **Sign in with another account**.

3. Admins are notified of the sign-up. Open **Settings → People & access**: they wait under **Waiting to join**.

4. Press **Approve** beside them, and confirm.

5. For more than a member's rights, press **···** beside them under **Members**, choose their role — *Member*, *Animal care*, *Facility manager* or *Admin* — and press **Set role**.
