They sign in with their own account and work as a member: they edit what they own and what is shared, and see the lab's databases. To share work with a few of them, put them in a [project group](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups).

> **Someone from outside the lab?** Give them a guest pass for a day to a month: **New guest pass** under **Guests** in **Settings → People & access**, who it's for and how long, **Make a code**. They open the link, enter the code, and work as a member with their own account until the pass ends or you press **End now**.

### Troubleshooting

#### They forgot their password

An admin resets it from the **···** beside them in **Settings → People & access**.

*Settings → People & access, where a new person is approved and given a role*

Related: [People and guests](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests) [Who can do what](https://biomanager.org/guide/who-can-do-what) [Run it for your lab](https://biomanager.org/server)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/invite-someone

---

## Lab setup

Turn databases on or off, and set your lab's name, time zone and dates.

Who and where: Admins only

After the first survey, the lab's setup is in **Settings**, under **Lab**. Admins change it; everyone else sees it, read only, so they know how the lab is set up. Each change is saved as you make it.

- **General** — the lab's name, time zone, dates, and weaning and genotyping days.

- **Databases** — switch each database and the calendar and notebook on or off; **Other databases** lists the ones made with **Add database** and members' own.

- **People & access** — the lab's people ([People and guests](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests)), its [project groups](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups), and **What members may do**: create their own databases, add ones for the whole lab, keep a copy of the lab, make tokens.

- **Statistics** — the lab's animals in numbers, by person, how full each rack and box is, and what is coming up. Admins choose there who may change each rack, box and incubator.

- **History** — the latest bulk changes, with **Undo**, and for admins the latest of every change ([Undo and history](https://biomanager.org/guide/undo-and-history)).

Switching a database off hides it and closes it to members, even by a saved link; its data is kept, and admins can still open it (a note says it is off).

Under **General**, besides its name:

- **Time zone** — what "today" and "overdue" mean, and the times shown. Blank uses the server's (or the computer's).

- **Dates** — how dates are written in lists and messages: *Sep 26, 2026*, *26 Sep 2026* or *2026-09-26*. Date fields you type into follow your computer's language.

- **Weaning day** — the day after birth a litter is due to be weaned (P21 unless you change it). Home, the calendar and the cage's **Wean due** date all follow it.

- **Genotyping day** — the day after birth the genotyping reminder falls on (P28 unless you change it).

### Troubleshooting

#### A database disappeared from the sidebar

An admin may have switched it off in **Settings → Databases**; its data is kept, and it comes back when it is switched on.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/lab-setup

---

## Your data and backups

Where your data is kept, how it's backed up, and how to move it.

### The desktop app

| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/` |
|---|---|
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\Biomanager\` |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/Biomanager/` |

- Your data lives outside the app, so updating or reinstalling never touches it.

- Before a new version changes the database an older one made, it copies it to `data/backups/before-upgrade-….db` in that folder, next to the database itself, `data/biomanager.db` (the last ten are kept). Every release is tested opening a lab made by each earlier release, with nothing lost.

- Back that folder up with Time Machine or File History, copying it while BioManager is closed.

> **Don't keep BioManager's data in Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive or iCloud Drive.** Syncing corrupts database files. BioManager warns you if it finds itself in one.

#### The whole lab in one file

**Settings → Your data → Save the whole lab** (admins) puts every record, account and uploaded file in one `.biomanager` file: in Downloads on the desktop app, downloaded from a server. It is a backup you can carry, and the way to bring the lab to another computer (**Moving to a new computer? Bring a lab file here** on a new desktop app's first page) or to a new server (**Bring a lab from the desktop app**). Stored connections such as Google Calendar links are left out: they are made again where the lab goes.

#### Labs set aside

**Start a new lab** (**Settings → Lab**, or the sign-in when nobody can sign in) sets the lab aside, whole, and opens an empty one. **Bring back a lab set aside** (**Settings → Lab**, the sign-in, or a new lab's first page) lists them with their names and accounts; the lab there now is set aside in its place, so either step can be undone the same way. Nothing is deleted.

### A lab server

A server backs up every night, restores the newest backup every week to prove it works, and can keep encrypted copies off-site — see [Keeping the data safe](https://biomanager.org/server#safe).

### The lab's key

Every lab has its own key. The server's nightly backups, **Save the whole lab** files and the copies on your computers are locked with it, so anyone who gets hold of one (a lost laptop, a backup disk, a file sent to the wrong person) sees only random bytes. The server, and the desktop apps of the lab's admins that join it, hold the key and open these files for you; you never type it in day to day.

- **Settings → Your data → Lab key** (admins) shows the key and when its recovery key was last shown, and to whom. **Show the recovery key** asks for your password, then shows it. Write it down or keep it in a password manager, away from the backups.

- If the server and every admin's computer were lost, the recovery key is the only way to open a backup. A new server restores with it ([Restore a backup](https://biomanager.org/guide/restore-a-backup#lab-server)), and a lab file or copy opens with it under **A lab back without its key** on the same page, or when you bring the lab file in.

- Anyone with the recovery key can read the lab's backups: keep it like the server's own password.

### A copy of the lab on your computer

When the desktop app joins your lab (**Open your lab**, below), it keeps a copy of the lab on that computer by itself, so the lab's records live on more than one machine: a fresh one every day while the app is open, checked, the last 14 kept, with the uploaded files mirrored. **Settings → Devices & copies** on the computer shows when the last copy was made.

A computer that shouldn't join can still keep a copy with a key: on the server, **Settings → Devices & copies**, name the computer and **Make a key** (shown once); in that computer's desktop app, enter the server's address and the key, and **Save and copy now**. (Admins always may; members when **Settings → People & access → What members may do** allows it.) **Revoke** stops a computer from taking more.

Each copy is locked with the lab's key and with that computer's own, so it opens on that computer and nowhere else without the recovery key. An admin's copy is the whole lab, and can rebuild the server if it's ever lost ([how](https://biomanager.org/server#move)): treat a computer holding one like the server itself. A member's copy holds what they can see in the app: no one's password, not other people's private notebook pages, personal databases or personal to-dos and events, not the Audit log. Guests can't keep a copy.

### One lab on many devices

One device holds the lab's **master copy**; every other one works on it through its address, so nothing is ever merged and nothing written in two places is lost. **Settings → Devices & copies → Devices** shows which device it is, and every computer linked to the lab: how it uses the lab, its version, when it was last heard from.

#### Your devices

Every computer, phone and browser you are signed in on is one of your devices, listed under **Your devices** in **Settings → Devices & copies**: what it is, when it was last seen and from where. Rename one by typing its new name; **Sign out** ends it there at once, without changing your password (a lost phone, a shared computer). Admins also see **Everyone's devices**.

- **The desktop app joins the lab as one of your devices.** **Open your lab** (on a new desktop app's first page, or **Go → Your Lab's BioManager**) finds the lab's address, then asks you to sign in as you do at the lab. Signed in with Google or Microsoft? **Use a code**: it shows a code to type under **A device shows a code?** on a computer or phone already signed in. The app's window then works on the lab through the app itself, never the server's page, and keeps its daily copy. **Go → This Computer's BioManager** comes back to its own lab, and **Go → Your Lab's BioManager** returns to the lab. **Sign out** in its window asks **Sign this computer out of the lab?**, which ends the device and forgets what it kept of the lab.

- **The phone apps** become one of your devices once you sign in through them, which lets them keep the facility on the phone for working without a signal ([Working offline](https://biomanager.org/guide/phones-and-cage-cards#offline)).

- **A browser** you sign in on is listed too; signing it out from another device signs it out there.

- **A lab server** is the master copy unless an admin hands it on.

- **Open the lab in this window** (a linked desktop): the app joins the lab as one of your devices, as above.

- **Share this lab on the network** (a desktop, admins): the computer becomes the master for every device on the same network, which opens the address it shows and signs in with an account there. It must stay on and awake. The connection isn't encrypted, so share only on a network you trust; for anywhere else, a lab server. Its own pages (setting up a server, its copies, its devices) are never offered to another device.

- **Make it the master** (on the master, admins): for a linked desktop with an admin's key, open now, on the same version. Within a minute it freezes the master (read only, so no change is lost), takes a last copy, keeps its own data in `backups/before-taking-over-….db`, and shares the lab on its network. The old master stays read only, with a banner pointing everyone there. Everyone signs in again with their lab account. Sign-ins to other services (Google Calendar) are not carried and are connected again.

- **Give the master copy back** (on the desktop holding it): its database and new files go back; the other device keeps what it had in `backups/before-taking-back-….db` and is the master again. The desktop turns read only and opens the lab there; **Go back to this computer's own lab** restores what it had before it took over.

- If the computer holding the master copy is lost, an admin on the old master chooses **Make this the master again**: what was changed on the lost computer since is not there.

### Getting your data out

**Export** on any sheet downloads what it shows as CSV, which opens in Excel. On the Mice sheet, **Export → Excel** is a workbook that **Import from Excel** reads back. A note that starts with `=` stays text in every export, never a formula. **Export my data** (in **Settings → Your data**) downloads your own mice, cages, weights, experiments and plasmids as CSV, each plasmid's sequence as a GenBank file with its features and the files kept with it, your notebook pages and your profile, in one zip.

### What BioManager sends its makers

Your records never leave your computer or your lab's server. BioManager is free, and a few anonymous counts are how its makers can show that labs rely on it and see which parts to improve first. Each installation sends one short message a day, with counts only:

- the version, whether it is the desktop app or a server, the operating system and the kind of database;

- how many members, and how many changed something this week, as ranges (1, 2–5, 6–15, 16–50, 51+);

- which built-in functions are on, and how many databases of each kind;

- a random id for the installation, so a lab counts once.

Never names, email addresses, anything anyone wrote, what your databases are called, or the computer's name or address. It goes to PostHog, which is asked not to work out where it came from. Admins see exactly what is sent on the **Usage report** (**Help → Send feedback → Usage report**). The counts are on unless an admin switches off **Share anonymous counts with BioManager's makers** in **Settings → General** (or **Switch off** on the Usage report). On a server, `BIOMANAGER_TELEMETRY=0` (or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`) in `.env` turns it off for good.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data

---

## Restore a backup

Put the desktop app's lab back as it was, from your own backup or from the copy BioManager kept before an update.

Who and where: Whoever uses that computer · Desktop app

1. Quit BioManager.

2. Open its data folder: `~/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/` on a Mac, `%APPDATA%\Biomanager\` on Windows, `~/.local/share/Biomanager/` on Linux. The lab's database is `data/biomanager.db`.

3. Move `data/biomanager.db` somewhere safe, rather than deleting it.

4. Put the backup in its place, named `biomanager.db`. From your Time Machine or File History copy of the folder; or one of the copies BioManager made before a new version changed the database, `data/backups/before-upgrade-….db` (the last ten are kept). Files added to records and pages are in the `uploads` folder; put it back from the same backup too.

5. Open BioManager. To undo an update, open it with the version you had before.

BioManager opens the lab as it was when that backup was made.

> **Newer changes aren't in a backup** Everything entered since the backup was made is not in it. Keep the file you moved aside until you are sure.

> **A lab set aside with Start a new lab** **Bring back a lab set aside** (**Settings → Lab**, the sign-in, or a new lab's first page) lists them; choose one and close BioManager, and it comes back the next time it opens. The lab there now is set aside in its place, so this can be undone the same way. They are kept in `data/old-labs/`.

### On a lab server

A server backs up every night and restores the newest backup every week to prove it works. Restoring is one command, run by whoever looks after the server, and never deletes what it replaces: see `deploy/RUNBOOK.md` in the server bundle and [Keeping the data safe](https://biomanager.org/server#safe). For a mistake in a bulk change, **Settings → History → Undo** is enough.

The backups are locked with [the lab's key](https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data#lab-key), so a backup that leaks can't be read. On the same server they open by themselves. On a new machine, which doesn't have the key, the restore is given the lab's recovery key (the runbook says how); once the lab is back, an admin enters the recovery key under **Settings → Your data → Lab key → A lab back without its key**, so the lab files and copies it locked open there again.

### Troubleshooting

#### BioManager won't start: the lab's database is an empty file

The file is 0 bytes, so its records are not in it. Put back a backup as above, or delete the empty file to start a new lab.

Related: [Your data and backups](https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data) [Undo and history](https://biomanager.org/guide/undo-and-history) [Keeping the data safe](https://biomanager.org/server#safe)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/restore-a-backup

---

## Scripts, instruments and other tools

Read and write your lab's data from scripts, R and instruments.

Who and where: Lab server or desktop

BioManager has an API: other programs can read the lab's records, and change them, as you. Pull an experiment's body weights straight into R or Python, have a balance post each weight as it weighs, let a core's system mark samples as done, or count cages for the facility — without anyone exporting a sheet.

1. **Settings → AI assistant & tokens**: say what will use it (*Balance in B12*, *My R scripts*), whether it may **Read**, **Read and change** or **Read and propose** (for an AI assistant: see below), and when it ends. **Make a token**.

2. Copy the token: it is shown once. Treat it like your password, and keep it out of scripts you share (an environment variable is the usual place).

3. Send it with each request, as `Authorization: Bearer bmt_…`. The **API reference** (the link on the same card, or `/api` on your BioManager) lists everything it can read and change, with examples in curl, Python and R.

- **A token is you.** It can do what you can on the pages, no more; a change made with it is in the change history under your name, marked with the token's name.

- It can read mice, cages, litters, strains, tanks and fish, plasmids, fly and worm vials, every inventory and every experiment; and change a mouse (its cage, genotype, note, status…), record a weight, change a vial, add or change an inventory item, and record an experiment's readout.

- A plasmid comes with its box, position and the glycerol stocks that carry it; its DNA sequence and map annotations, which can run to many thousands of letters, only when asked: `/api/v1/plasmids/14?sequence=1`. A litter names the cage its pups are in, and `/api/v1/litters?cage=88` lists the litters in cage 88.

- For a tool that starts from your own words (an AI assistant, say), it can also find the records a phrase means, each with a reference to use (`/api/v1/resolve?q=cage 88`), list what your lab calls things: strains, statuses, purposes, racks, people and each database's own fields (`/api/v1/vocabulary`), and list what is due, as Home does (`/api/v1/due`).

- Make one token for each thing that uses it, so you can **Revoke** one without the others. The card shows when each was last used. Admins see everyone's tokens and can revoke any; **Members may make API tokens**, under **What members may do** in **Settings → People & access**, can keep them to admins.

- With the desktop app, only programs on that computer can reach it; on a lab server, anything that can reach the server.

### Changes an assistant proposes

A token that may **Read and propose** is for an AI assistant: it changes nothing itself, and sends its changes as one proposal that you approve, whole, under **Proposed changes**. Connecting one and approving are in [AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants).

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/scripts-and-api

---

## AI assistants

Tell an AI assistant what you did, or ask it to plan; it proposes the records, and you approve them in BioManager.

Who and where: Lab server or desktop

BioManager has no AI inside it. If you already use an assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Cherry Studio or another app that speaks MCP), you can connect it to your lab. Tell it what you did, in your own words or with a photo of your notebook (*litter in 102 yesterday, 7 pups; moved the two old breeders from 88 to 91; injected day 3 of the TMX cohort this morning*), and it turns that into records: as one proposal, which you approve in BioManager. It never changes anything itself.

### Connect an assistant

Open **Help → Connect an AI assistant** (also under **Settings → AI assistant & tokens**). It shows the ways in for your BioManager, with its address filled in. Step by step for each app, with what to check first: [Connect an AI assistant](https://biomanager.org/guide/connect-an-ai-assistant).

Add the **BioManager plugin** to your assistant too, once (Claude, Codex, VS Code, Qwen Code; from `gaspolymerase/biomanager`; Kimi Code from its own download). It teaches the assistant how to work with BioManager, so you never have to explain it: say what you did, or just *I want to change something in BioManager*, and it shows you what's due today and asks what you did.

### What to say

Talk to it as you would to a colleague who keeps the records. The plugin also gives your assistant these commands (in Claude, type `/`):

| Log today's work | *Weaned 110, weighed 6 and 7, moved 30 and 31 to 106.* It looks up each animal, cage and experiment, asks when something could be more than one record, and sends one proposal. |
|---|---|
| Log from a photo | A photo of your notebook, the whiteboard or cage cards. It reads the numbers, asks about any it can't read, and proposes. |
| Process my captures | What you wrote down or photographed at the bench ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#captures)) becomes records. |
| Plan tomorrow | What's due, grouped by room and time, overdue first. |
| Review the lab this week | The week's checks ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#review)), and one proposal for the clean-up. |
| Design an experiment | From a question to a planned experiment ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#plan)). |
| Write the methods | A methods paragraph and the ARRIVE checklist for an experiment, from its records ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#write)). |
| Animal-use report | The animals used under each protocol over the year, for the annual review ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#write)). |
| Write a handover | Everything someone leaving looks after, and what is due on it ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#write)). |

You can also just ask: *Which lot of tamoxifen did cohort 3 get?*, *Where's the last tube of pAAV-hSyn-GCaMP8m?*, *Who changed cage 88's purpose?* It searches your records and notebook, reads a record's history and a plasmid's or a mouse's family tree, and answers with links. It reads only what you can read. Upload a clone's sequencing read (`.ab1`) as a capture and ask *does clone 3 match plasmid 14?*: BioManager checks it against the map, as [Verify sequencing](https://biomanager.org/guide/plasmids#verify) does, and the assistant tells you each difference and what it does to the protein.

### Captures: write it down now, record it later

At the rack you rarely have time for a conversation. **Capture** keeps what you'd tell the assistant until you have:

- On a phone, open **Captures** in your account menu and press **New capture**, or press **Capture** in an experiment's **Bench mode**. Type, or use the keyboard's microphone to dictate; add a photo with **Take photo**, or a file (a balance's or plate reader's CSV, or a sequencing read) with **Choose file**; **Scan a card** attaches the cage, tank or vial it's about. **Save**.

- Later, at your desk, tell the assistant *process my captures*. It reads each, photos and files included, and sends one proposal; each change says which capture it came from.

- **Captures** lists yours, waiting ones first. Approving a proposal marks the captures it used as used, with the proposal; **Dismiss** sets one aside (**Keep it waiting** brings it back). Only you see your captures.

### What it can propose

- In the mouse colony, zebrafish, fly and worm databases and any other organism's: the everyday records. New animals, cages, tanks and vials; litters (with how many pups were born), weaning, moves and deaths; crosses, clutches and flips; weights and readings; scheduled jobs done.

- In your inventories: a new item, a change, an amount used (the item turns low at its **Low at**; say it in another unit of weight or volume, *40 mg* of an item kept in g, and BioManager converts it; *2 mL* of one kept in ampoules once it has a **Pack size**), an order received (and added to stock under the name, amount and unit your stock keeps), a sample taken from an animal; and an inventory renumbered, so each # is the number in its name (**Renumber**, [below](https://biomanager.org/guide/samples-and-orders#every-inventory)).

- In plasmids: a new plasmid (with its sequence pasted as GenBank or FASTA), a change, a glycerol stock, a primer or a primer pair.

- In an experiment: a step done (with the reagent and lot used: the step's own, unless you name another bottle or lot; an unknown lot is refused, and with several bottles of the same name it asks which), a readout, animals added, its status, a note; and a new, **planned** experiment ([below](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants#plan)).

- In the notebook: a line in today's daily log; a new page (marked *Drafted by* the assistant, never signed); a section added to a page, unless someone has it open. To fix a page it made, or one of yours, it changes that page rather than making another: its title, kind, tags, or its text, all of it or a few parts (steps rewritten as a checklist, so **Run** can tick them off). You see each change before and after; the text as it was is kept in the page's **History**, and a signed page, or one someone has open, is left alone. It can also make a folder in **Protocols** and file protocols in it.

- In the calendar: an event, or an instrument booking.

- It can't delete anything, sign a page, start an experiment, or change who may see what.

### Planning: breeding, cohorts, experiments

For anything with a right answer, the assistant asks BioManager, which works it out from your lab's own records, and tells you the assumptions:

- **Which animals are free**: by genotype, sex and age on a date, leaving out those in experiments and breeding cages.

- **A breeding plan**: *I need 12 Cre⁺ fl/fl males at 8 weeks by March 1.* The odds for each mating, from the breeders you have; how many matings to set up, and by when, counting every litter a mating has time for and the pairs already in Breeding cages; your line's own litter sizes; up to five genes. It says when two of the crosses it lists would need the same breeders, and which breeders are in an experiment. A strain (C57BL/6J, BALB/c) isn't an allele: wanting it means both parents of that strain.

- **Animals per group**: from the difference you want to see and the spread in your own past readouts (the same numbers G*Power gives).

- **Random groups**: balanced for sex and litter, with weights even across groups; the seed is kept, in a new experiment's description.

- **When stock runs out**: from how fast each item has been used.

- **Readouts from raw numbers**: a caliper sheet, a qPCR export or a plate-reader file becomes tumour volumes, ΔΔCt and fold change, or blank-subtracted ODs, worked out by BioManager and shown to you before it proposes them ([Experiments](https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments#derived)).

- **A plate on its layout**: give it the plate reader's or qPCR machine's export (or a capture of its file), and it is read onto the experiment's plate layout: each animal's wells averaged, the replicates far from the others and the wells past what the instrument reads named, and the readings proposed for you to approve ([Experiments](https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments#plates)).

**Designing an experiment.** Tell it the question (*does deleting Il33 in airway epithelium reduce inflammation in our HDM model? Start in about six weeks*). It proposes the groups and controls, the main readout, how many animals and which, the regimen from your saved regimens, and the test, and says what it assumed. Doses for something the lab hasn't used come with a source, and checking the design against your animal protocol is yours. Approved, it is a **planned** experiment: nothing is due until you press **Start**, and after that, changes to the plan ask why ([Experiments](https://biomanager.org/guide/experiments#planned)).

### A weekly review

*Review the lab this week* runs BioManager's checks: overdue jobs, the animals that may need a look (losing weight past the lab's threshold, notes with a welfare word, not weighed in an experiment, status and experiment disagreeing: the same as Home's card, [Home](https://biomanager.org/guide/home-page#animals)), empty cages still in a rack, breeders past 30 weeks, notebook pages left unsigned, reagents expired, expiring or low, and proposals still waiting. It sums them up by how much they matter and offers one proposal for what can be cleaned up (a mouse in an active experiment whose status says *geno* gets its status set to *experiment*). For an animal it says what the records show, with the numbers and the note's own line, never a diagnosis. An admin or lab manager can have their assistant run it every Monday (in Claude, as a scheduled task).

### Write-ups

*Write the methods for the TMX cohort* gives a methods paragraph built only from the records: strains, sex, age and numbers per group, each manipulation with its dose, route, days and lot (and any lot used after it expired), the readout and the tests. With it comes the ARRIVE 2.0 Essential 10, each item with what the records say and what's missing, and the experiment's changes from its plan. It can put the draft in a new notebook page, marked as drafted by the assistant.

**The animal-use report.** *Draft our animal-use report for protocol 2024-0012* gives, for the last twelve months (or the dates you say), a table per protocol of the mice, zebrafish and your own organisms by strain: how many were born, added to the records, used in experiments, died or were euthanized (with the reasons their notes give) and kept for breeding. BioManager does the counting, and the report says what each number is based on and what the records can't say, such as animals with no protocol. A mouse's protocol is the colony's own protocol column (add one under **Configure → Your own columns**, called *IACUC #* or *Protocol*), else, for a pup, its mother's or father's; pups a litter counted that have no record of their own are under their parents' protocol too. A fish's is its line's **IACUC #**; another organism's is its own **Protocol**, else its housing's, else its line's. It is a draft to check against your institution's form.

**A handover.** *Write a handover for me* before you leave (an admin can ask for anyone's) lists everything in your name: cages and mice by rack and position, breeding cages and what's due on them, tanks, vials, inventory items and glycerol stocks with where each is, plasmids, experiments and their next steps, racks and boxes you made, notebook pages not signed and proposals waiting, each with its link, then everything due in the next 30 days. Ask it to, and it proposes giving the records to whoever takes them over (as **Set field → Owner** would); someone else's notebook pages stay theirs, counted but not named.

### Approving

A proposal tells you (the bell) and waits under **Proposed changes** in your account menu.

- Each proposal is one summary in plain words, with any warnings at the top (a litter date that would be replaced, pups too young to wean, a cage that would stop being shared with the lab, an item of that name already in stock), then one line for each change, its database's icon beside it. On the right of a line is what it came from: *You said* (point at it to read your words), or *Photo* and the line of the page it read. **Show each change** lists every record, before → after, with your words for each change.

- **Approve** makes every change at once; **Discard** makes none. If something is wrong, **Send back** with a line saying what: the assistant reads it and proposes again, corrected, and the new proposal takes the old one's place.

- An approved proposal is one batch in **Batch history**, marked with the assistant's name, so **Undo** takes it back whole (a line added to the notebook stays).

- If a record it touches was changed after the proposal was made, or a change no longer goes through, nothing is applied and the page says which record and why.

- Only you can approve your proposals, and only signed in to BioManager: no token can. A proposal you leave waits two weeks, then expires.

### Troubleshooting

#### The assistant can't reach BioManager, or doesn't seem to know it

See [Connect an AI assistant](https://biomanager.org/guide/connect-an-ai-assistant#troubleshooting).

#### Approving says a record changed after the proposal was made

Someone (or you) changed it meanwhile, so the proposal may be out of date. **Discard** it and ask the assistant to propose again.

#### It worked out a number itself

Ask it to use BioManager's tool for it (breeding plan, animals per group, groups), and to say the assumptions. With the plugin it does so on its own.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants

---

## Connect an AI assistant

Step by step for each assistant app: add the BioManager plugin once, connect it to your lab, sign in, and try it.

Who and where: Lab server or desktop

Connecting takes a few minutes, once. Whatever app you use, it is the same four steps:

1. **Check that your app can reach BioManager** (the table below).

2. **Add the BioManager plugin**, where your app takes plugins. It teaches the assistant how to work with BioManager, so you never have to explain it.

3. **Connect it to your lab** with your BioManager's address, and **sign in**: BioManager opens in your browser and you press **Allow**. There is no password or token to give the assistant.

4. **Try it**: say *I want to change something in BioManager*.

Everything you need is on **Help → Connect an AI assistant** in BioManager (also under **Settings → AI assistant & tokens**), with your lab's address filled in, buttons for some apps and commands to copy for others. Keep it open beside this page.

### Can your app reach BioManager?

An assistant app connects either from your own computer or from its company's servers on the internet. Which one decides what it can reach:

| Your BioManager | Apps on your computer | Apps in the cloud |
|---|---|---|
| The desktop app, on this computer | Yes | No |
| A lab server, on the lab network only | Yes, from a computer on the lab network | No |
| A lab server on the internet | Yes | Yes |

- **On your computer**: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Cherry Studio, QwenWork (千问办公), Trae, Doubao (豆包) on the computer, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, and Claude Desktop with a token.

- **In the cloud**: claude.ai with the Claude desktop and phone apps' chats, and ChatGPT. They need the lab's server on the internet; its admin turns that on (the server's runbook, *internet access*). Until then, the Connect page says so and shows only the other ways.

The Connect page shows two addresses, both ending in `/api/v1/mcp`: the **connector address** (on the internet, for the cloud apps) and the address for apps **on this computer or the lab network**.

### Claude

#### Claude on the web, the desktop app and the phone

Needs the lab's server on the internet. Do these on claude.ai or in the desktop app; the phone app then has it too.

1. **Add the plugin.** Open **Customize → Plugins**, choose **Add → Add marketplace**, enter `gaspolymerase/biomanager`, then open **BioManager** and press **Add**. Or download **Plugin for Claude** from the [Download page](https://biomanager.org/download#ai-plugin) and choose **Add → Upload plugin** with the zip. Once BioManager is listed in Claude's directory, you can find it under **Discover** instead.

2. **Add the connector.** Open the plugin's **Connectors** tab (or **Customize → Connectors**), choose **Add custom connector**, name it *BioManager*, and paste the **connector address** from the Connect page.

3. **Connect.** Press **Connect**. A BioManager page opens asking for a **connection code**. On the Connect page (on the lab network), press **Get a connection code**, type the code in, and press **Allow**. A code works once, for 10 minutes.

4. **Try it.** In a new chat, check BioManager is on in the chat's tools menu, and say *I want to change something in BioManager*. The first time, Claude asks before it uses each tool; choose **Always allow** for BioManager's tools. They can only read and propose: nothing changes until you approve it in BioManager.

> **On a Team or Enterprise plan** An owner adds the connector for the organization, and can install the plugin for everyone (**Installed by default**). Each person then only connects, with their own connection code, so the assistant works as them.

#### Claude Code

Works with the desktop app and with a server on the lab network. In Claude Code:

1. Type `/plugin marketplace add gaspolymerase/biomanager`, then `/plugin install biomanager@biomanager`.

2. It asks for **BioManager's MCP address**: paste the address for **this computer or the lab network** from the Connect page.

3. Type `/mcp`, choose *biomanager* and **Authenticate**. BioManager opens in your browser: press **Allow**.

4. Say *I want to change something in BioManager*.

Without the plugin, the Connect page's one command connects it (`claude mcp add …`), or press **Copy the message** and send it to Claude Code: it sets itself up.

#### Claude Desktop, with a desktop app or a lab-network server

Claude Desktop's own connectors come from the internet, so for a BioManager it can't reach that way, it runs a small program from BioManager's source instead. On the Connect page, press **Make a token**: the next page shows the setup to paste into Claude Desktop (**Settings → Developer → Edit Config**), with your address and token in it. The steps, and the one command that installs what it needs, are in `mcp/README.md`. Claude Desktop's **Code** tab is Claude Code, and connects as above.

### ChatGPT and Codex

#### ChatGPT

Needs the lab's server on the internet, and ChatGPT on the web: ChatGPT's phone apps don't take your own servers. ChatGPT lets a **Business, Enterprise or Edu** workspace make changes this way, once its admin turns on developer mode; on other plans it can only read.

1. Open **Plugins**, press **+** and choose **Add custom MCP server**.

2. Name it *BioManager*, paste the **connector address**, choose **OAuth**, and confirm with **I understand and want to continue**, then **Create as a plugin** and install it.

3. When it asks you to sign in, a BioManager page asks for a **connection code**: get one on the Connect page, type it in, and press **Allow**.

4. To have ChatGPT know BioManager without explaining it, add the plugin too: download **Plugin for ChatGPT** from the [Download page](https://biomanager.org/download#ai-plugin), upload it at **platform.openai.com/plugins** and share it with your lab; each person then installs it. If someone in your lab already shared it with you, just install it.

5. In a chat, choose BioManager (type `@`) and say *I want to change something in BioManager*. Under its permissions, **Allow read actions** stops it asking before every look-up.

#### Codex

1. Add the plugin: `codex plugin marketplace add gaspolymerase/biomanager`, then install *BioManager* from its plugins.

2. Connect: `codex mcp add biomanager --url <address>` with the address for **this computer or the lab network** (the Connect page has the command with it filled in).

3. Sign in: `codex mcp login biomanager`. BioManager opens in your browser: press **Allow**.

### Cursor and VS Code

1. On the Connect page, press **Add to Cursor** or **Add to VS Code**. The app opens and asks before adding BioManager: accept.

2. Sign in: the app shows that BioManager *needs login*, or asks you to allow it; BioManager opens in your browser, press **Allow**.

3. In VS Code, also add the plugin: run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** with `https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager`.

### Assistants used in China

The DeepSeek, Qwen (千问) and Kimi chat apps can't connect to other apps yet. These can, from a computer that reaches BioManager.

#### Cherry Studio, with DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi or GLM

1. Set up Cherry Studio with your model's key (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi or Zhipu GLM), as Cherry Studio describes.

2. On the Connect page, press **Add to Cherry Studio**. Cherry Studio opens with BioManager added, switched off: switch it on in **Settings → MCP**.

3. Sign in when BioManager opens in your browser: press **Allow**.

4. In a chat, turn on the BioManager tools and say *I want to change something in BioManager*.

#### QwenWork (千问办公), Trae and Doubao (豆包)

These take your BioManager's address with a token. On the Connect page, press **Make a token**; the next page shows the setup, with the address and token filled in.

- **QwenWork**: **扩展 → 连接器 → + 添加 → 粘贴 JSON 配置**, and paste the JSON.

- **Trae**: **设置 → MCP → 添加 → 手动添加**, and paste the same JSON.

- **Doubao** on the computer: **技能 · 连接器 → 新建 → 新建自定义连接器**, transport **HTTP**, the address, and a header `Authorization` with the value `Bearer` and the token.

The token is shown once: keep it in the app, not in a note. Revoke it under **Settings → AI assistant & tokens** when you stop using the app.

#### Qwen Code and Kimi Code

- **Qwen Code**: add the plugin with `qwen extensions install https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager:biomanager`, then connect with `qwen mcp add --transport http biomanager <address>`. It signs in by itself in your browser.

- **Kimi Code**: add the plugin with `/plugins install https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/BioManager-plugin-Kimi.zip`, and confirm when it asks. Then type `/mcp-config` and add an HTTP server named `biomanager` with the address (or put `{"mcpServers": {"biomanager": {"url": "<address>"}}}` in `~/.kimi-code/mcp.json`). Sign in with `/mcp-config login biomanager`: BioManager opens in your browser, press **Allow**. Then type `/new` and say *I want to change something in BioManager*. The plugin's prompts are under `/biomanager:`, such as `/biomanager:log-today`.

- The older **kimi-cli** takes no plugins: connect with `kimi mcp add -t http biomanager <address> --auth oauth`, then `kimi mcp auth biomanager`.

#### Claude Code on DeepSeek or GLM

DeepSeek and Zhipu (GLM) both offer an address that speaks Claude's API, so Claude Code, with the BioManager plugin, can run on a DeepSeek or Zhipu key. Set Claude Code up as their own pages say (DeepSeek's *Anthropic API* guide, Zhipu's *Claude Code* guide), then follow [Claude Code](https://biomanager.org/guide/connect-an-ai-assistant#claude-code) above.

### Any other app

An app that takes an MCP server (Goose, OpenCode, LobeHub, Chatbox and others) needs the address, as a **streamable HTTP** server. If it signs in with OAuth, leave the headers empty and sign in in the browser; if it doesn't, press **Make a token** and give it the header the next page shows. An app that only starts commands runs `mcp/biomanager_mcp.py`, as for Claude Desktop.

### Check that it works

1. Say *I want to change something in BioManager*. It should show you what's due today and ask what you did, without asking you how BioManager works.

2. Tell it one small real thing, e.g. *weighed mouse 1043, 24.1 g*. It looks the mouse up, sends one proposal, and gives you a link.

3. Open the link (or the bell) in BioManager: the proposal waits under **Proposed changes**. Read it, and press **Approve** or **Discard**.

The connection is listed under **Settings → AI assistant & tokens** with the app's name. Revoke it there to end it; the assistant then can't read anything.

### Troubleshooting

#### The assistant doesn't seem to know BioManager

Check that BioManager is on in the chat's tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Cherry Studio switch tools per chat), and that the plugin is added and turned on. Without the plugin, say *use BioManager's lab_overview first*.

#### It can't reach BioManager

For apps on your computer: check that BioManager is running and that the address is the one for **this computer or the lab network**. For claude.ai and ChatGPT: the **connector address** should open from a phone off the lab's Wi-Fi, showing a short message asking for an API token. If it doesn't, the server isn't on the internet yet.

#### Connecting says the connection code isn't right

A code works once and for 10 minutes. Press **Get a connection code** again and use the new one.

#### ChatGPT can read but not propose

On ChatGPT plans other than Business, Enterprise and Edu, your own servers can only read. Use another app to propose, or ask your workspace's admin about developer mode.

#### Every few weeks it asks me to sign in again

A sign-in lasts 90 days without use. Sign in again the same way; nothing else is lost.

Related: [AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants) [Scripts and the API](https://biomanager.org/guide/scripts-and-api) [Run it for your lab](https://biomanager.org/server)

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/connect-an-ai-assistant

---

## Troubleshooting

Common problems and their fixes, each also on the page it belongs to.

- **The app won't open on my Mac**: Right-click it and choose **Open**. If macOS says it's damaged, move it to Applications first, then try again. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/install)

- **Linux: the AppImage does nothing**: Mark it executable. If it still won't start, install `libfuse2`, or use the `.tar.gz` and run `BioManager/BioManager`. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/install)

- **My phone can't reach the server**: Check the address with your admin; that you're on the lab's network, VPN or Tailscale; and, if your lab uses its own certificate, that it's installed on the phone. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/phones-and-cage-cards)

- **I can't edit a record**: It belongs to someone else and isn't shared: BioManager says whose it is. Ask them, or an admin. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/who-can-do-what)

- **A cell turned red**: That change wasn't saved; the message at the bottom says why (a required field, a date that isn't one). [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/sheets)

- **I made a mistake with a bulk change**: **Settings → History** → **Undo**. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/undo-and-history)

- **I forgot my password**: Ask an admin: the **···** beside you in **Settings → People & access** resets it. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests)

- **My new account is waiting for an admin to approve it**: Only a lab's first account is its admin; later ones wait for its approval. On the desktop app, an account was made on this computer before: sign in with that one. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests)

- **Nobody can sign in to the lab on my computer**: On the desktop app, **Start a new lab** on the sign-in page sets the lab aside, without deleting anything, and starts an empty one; **Bring back a lab set aside** undoes it. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests)

- **Rows were skipped on import**: The preview lists each one by its row number in Excel and says why. Fix those rows and import just them: importing the whole sheet again would add the other rows a second time. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/bring-your-lab-in)

- **A colleague's database isn't in my sidebar**: It may be their personal one (*Just you* on its tile), which only they and admins see, or an admin may have switched it off. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/any-organism)

- **A database disappeared from the sidebar**: An admin may have switched it off in **Settings → Databases**; its data is kept, and it comes back when it is switched on. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/lab-setup)

- **Something else**: **Help → Send feedback** in the sidebar (see below), or [open an issue](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/issues) — say which system you use and what you expected to happen.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/troubleshooting

---

## Feedback

Send feedback to your lab's admins from any page, or open it as a GitHub issue for BioManager's makers.

**Send feedback**, under Help in the sidebar, is for something that went wrong, an idea or a question, from the page you're on. It is kept in your lab: its admins are told, read it on the same page and mark it **Done**. To tell BioManager's makers too, **Open as a GitHub issue**: a new issue opens with your text, the page, the version and the browser filled in (not your server's address, nor your name), for you to check and submit. You need a GitHub account.

Admins also find a **Usage report** there: for each of the last eight weeks, how many people changed something and how many changes in each area, and what the lab holds now. Counts only — no names, nothing anyone wrote — and the report is not sent anywhere: copy the text at the bottom into an email, for instance to whoever runs a pilot with your lab. Below it, **Anonymous counts for BioManager's makers** shows the daily message word for word, with **Switch off** ([more](https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data#counts)).

### On GitHub

You can also go straight to BioManager's GitHub page and [open an issue](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/issues/new/choose): **Something isn't working** or **An idea or something missing**. Leave out names, lab data, passwords and your server's address. If BioManager helps your lab, [a star on GitHub](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager) helps other labs find it.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/feedback

---

Source: https://biomanager.org/deploy-with-ai.md

# Deploying BioManager: a guide for AI assistants

You are helping someone set up **BioManager**, a lab database for animal
colonies, stocks and inventories, as a server for their lab. This file is
written for you: follow it in order, run the checks, and stop where it says
to ask. The human-readable version is
https://biomanager.org/server.

## Rules

1. **Secrets never pass through the chat.** Passwords, API keys, the
   PostgreSQL password, OAuth client secrets, Backblaze keys, SSH private
   keys: have the person type or paste them directly on the server (in
   `nano .env`, or at a prompt), or generate them there with
   `openssl rand -hex 24`. Do not echo `.env` back into the conversation.
   If you must confirm a value is set, check it is non-empty:
   `grep -c '^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.\+' .env`.
2. **Ask before anything that costs money, can't be undone, or opens the
   server to the internet**: creating cloud resources, upgrading a cloud
   account, buying a domain, opening firewall ports, `internet-access.sh on`,
   restoring a backup, `docker compose down -v` (that deletes the database).
3. **Accounts are theirs.** The person creates cloud, Tailscale, domain and
   OAuth accounts and signs in to them in their own browser. You tell them
   what to click.
4. **Back up before changing a running server:**
   `docker compose exec backup backup.sh`.
5. **Never expose PostgreSQL.** Only Caddy publishes ports (80, 443, and
   8081 on 127.0.0.1 only). Do not add ports to `db` or `app`.
6. After each step, run its **check**. If a check fails, fix that before
   going on; the troubleshooting table below covers the usual causes.

## First, ask

Ask these, then recommend an option (the table after them) and wait for a yes.

1. Who will use it: one person, or a lab (how many people)?
2. Where are they: all in one building on the same network, or also at home,
   on phones on mobile data, or at other sites?
3. Is there a computer that can stay on (and does IT allow running a server
   on the network), or would they rather use a free cloud VM?
4. Do they want an ordinary web address that needs no app (a domain,
   about $10–15 a year), or is installing Tailscale on each device fine?
5. Do they have the desktop app's data already, to move onto the server?
6. Their time zone (for backups and dates).

| Situation | Option |
| --- | --- |
| One person | **A**: the desktop app. No server. Send them to https://biomanager.org/download and stop here. |
| One building, a Linux computer that stays on | **B**: a Linux computer in the lab, `TLS=internal` (or `TLS=files` with IT's certificate). For a Mac, send them to the desktop app: Settings → Set up a lab server → This computer, for the whole lab |
| University offers VMs | **C**: ask IT for a VM with Docker, a DNS name and a certificate; then as B with `TLS=files` |
| People anywhere, most labs | **D**: Ubuntu 24.04 cloud VM + Tailscale, `TLS=tailscale` (recommended; free on Oracle Cloud Always Free) |
| An address that works with no app | **E**: cloud VM + a domain, `TLS=acme`, ports 80/443 open |

## Facts

- **What runs:** four Docker containers from the server bundle: `app`
  (gunicorn, image `ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager:<version>`), `db`
  (PostgreSQL 16, internal network only), `caddy` (HTTPS), `backup`
  (nightly `pg_dump` + uploads tarball, weekly restore test, optional
  restic off-site).
- **The bundle:**
  `https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz`.
  It unpacks to `Biomanager/deploy/`; always unpack it into
  `/opt/biomanager`, so the deploy folder is
  `/opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy` (scripts and systemd units assume it).
  `BUNDLE.md`, `README.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` inside are the reference.
- **The app image** is not pulled from a registry: the same release has
  `biomanager-image-amd64.tar.gz` and `biomanager-image-arm64.tar.gz`, and
  `deploy/host/load-image.sh` downloads the one for this machine (for the
  version in `deploy/VERSION`) and `docker load`s it with the tag
  `compose.yaml` expects. Run it after every unpack, before `docker compose up`.
  Check: `docker image ls ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager` shows the version.
- **Settings:** `deploy/.env` (from `.env.example`, mode 600). Required:
  `DOMAIN`, `TLS` (`internal` | `tailscale` | `acme` | `files`),
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (letters and digits only). Usual: `TZ`,
  `BACKUP_DIR=/opt/biomanager/backups`, `BACKUP_TIME=02:30`, `KEEP_LOCAL=30`.
  With `TLS=tailscale` also `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.tailscale.yaml`.
  With `TLS=acme` also `ACME_EMAIL`. Optional: `RESTIC_*`/`AWS_*` (off-site,
  set by `host/offsite-setup.sh`), `HEALTHCHECK_PING_URL`,
  `BIOMANAGER_GOOGLE_*`/`BIOMANAGER_MICROSOFT_*` (sign-in), `BIOMANAGER_OIDC_*` (the
  institution's own sign-in, OpenID Connect) or `BIOMANAGER_CILOGON_*` (a SAML-only
  university, through CILogon), SMTP, `BIOMANAGER_TELEMETRY=0` (never send
  BioManager's makers the anonymous daily counts; ask the admin, who can
  also switch them off on the Usage report).
- **First account:** the app prints a one-time setup code in its log; the
  first account created at `https://DOMAIN/register` with it is the admin.
  Later sign-ups wait for an admin's approval.
- **Resources:** 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk is plenty. ARM (Oracle Ampere)
  and x86-64 both work.
- **Host extras (Linux with systemd):** `sudo host/install.sh` (from the
  deploy folder) installs a watchdog (every 5 min: site, containers, disk, backups),
  weekly image updates and the updater behind **Update now** in the app's Settings
  (`host/update.sh`, started by `biomanager-update.path`), alerting to an ntfy topic it prints.
  `host/offsite-setup.sh` sets up encrypted off-site backups (asks for the
  key itself). `host/internet-access.sh on|off|status` opens temporary guest
  access via Tailscale Funnel (option D only).

## Option D: cloud VM + Tailscale (recommended)

**D1. Accounts (the person does these).** Oracle Cloud (free tier; home
region can't be changed later) and Tailscale. Ask them to download the
bundle to their own computer too, and open
`Biomanager/deploy/cloud-init.yaml`.

**D2. The VM (the person clicks; you guide).** Compute → Instances →
Create: Ubuntu 24.04; shape VM.Standard.A1.Flex (2 OCPU/12 GB or 4/24); a
public subnet with a public IPv4; their SSH public key (help them run
`ssh-keygen -t ed25519` if they have none; only the `.pub` goes to Oracle);
Advanced → Management → Initialization script: the contents of
`cloud-init.yaml`. "Out of capacity" means try again later or another
availability domain. Any other provider's Ubuntu 24.04 VM works the same;
then run the steps of `cloud-init.yaml`'s `runcmd` by hand if it has no
cloud-init box.

**D3. Tailscale.**

```bash
ssh ubuntu@<public IP>
test -f /var/lib/biomanager-ready && echo ready    # wait for cloud-init
sudo tailscale up --hostname=biomanager            # the person opens the printed link
```

The person, in the Tailscale admin console: Machines → biomanager →
Disable key expiry; DNS → enable MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates. Ask them
for the tailnet name (`tailXXXX.ts.net`); it is not secret.
Check: `tailscale status` lists the machine; from their computer, with
Tailscale on, `ssh ubuntu@biomanager` works. Continue over that connection
(a fresh login also puts `ubuntu` in the `docker` group cloud-init added it to).

**D4. BioManager.**

```bash
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/biomanager-server.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz
tar -xzf /tmp/biomanager-server.tar.gz -C /opt/biomanager
cd /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy
host/load-image.sh
cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)|" .env
sed -i "s|^TLS=.*|TLS=tailscale|; s|^#COMPOSE_FILE=|COMPOSE_FILE=|; s|^BACKUP_DIR=.*|BACKUP_DIR=/opt/biomanager/backups|" .env
sed -i "s|^DOMAIN=.*|DOMAIN=biomanager.tailXXXX.ts.net|; s|^TZ=.*|TZ=<their time zone>|" .env
grep -E '^(DOMAIN|TLS|COMPOSE_FILE|TZ|BACKUP_DIR)=' .env
host/ports.sh
docker compose config --quiet && echo "settings ok"
docker compose up -d --build
```

`host/ports.sh` writes `HTTP_PORT`, `HTTPS_PORT` and `FUNNEL_PORT` into
`.env`: 80, 443 and 8081 when free, others when the machine already uses
them. If it says another port (`BioManager will be at https://…:4443`),
that address, port included, is the one to give everyone below.

Check: `docker compose ps` shows `db` and `app` healthy within a minute or
two, and `backup` healthy once its first backup is done (`health: starting`
until then); `curl -fsS https://biomanager.tailXXXX.ts.net/healthz` prints `ok`;
`docker compose exec backup ls /backups/db` lists a first dump.
Then `docker compose logs app | grep "setup code"`: the person opens
`https://DOMAIN/register` on a device with Tailscale and creates the admin
account with it. The code is single-use; it is fine to show it to them.

**D5. Host extras.** `sudo host/install.sh` (in the deploy folder); tell them to subscribe
to the printed ntfy topic in the ntfy app. Check:
`systemctl list-timers 'biomanager-*'` and `systemctl is-active biomanager-update.path`.

**D6. Close the door (ask first).** In Oracle Cloud, delete the security
list's ingress rule for port 22. Check from their computer:
`ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 ubuntu@<public IP>` times out, while
`ssh ubuntu@biomanager` keeps working over Tailscale.

**D6b. Oracle's idle stop (optional; ask first).** Oracle stops an Always
Free VM that looks idle for a week (starting it again loses nothing).
Upgrading the account to Pay As You Go (Billing) stops that and still bills
nothing for Always Free resources.

**D7. Off-site backups (recommended; ask first).** The person creates a
Backblaze B2 bucket (private, encryption on, Object Lock on with a 30-day
Governance default) and an application key limited to that bucket. Then,
in their own terminal (the script asks for the key and shows the backup
password once, to save in their password manager):
`ssh -t biomanager sudo /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy/host/offsite-setup.sh`.

**D8. The lab.** Members install Tailscale; the person either invites them
to the tailnet or shares the one machine with their own Tailscale accounts
(Machines → biomanager → Share). Members sign up at the address; the admin
approves them in Settings → People & access. Phones: Android app (download page), or on
iPhone Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen.

## Options B and C: a Linux computer or a university VM

As D4 with `TLS=internal` (B; or `TLS=files` for C, with IT's certificate
and key copied to `deploy/certs/server.crt` and `deploy/certs/server.key`),
`DOMAIN` = a fixed IP or a DNS name that never changes, and no
`COMPOSE_FILE`. Docker: `curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh`
(then `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER` and log in again); turn off sleep.
By hand this is Linux only (the scripts, timers and `/opt` paths assume
it); on a Mac, the desktop app's Settings → Set up a lab server → This
computer, for the whole lab does it. Create `/opt/biomanager` owned by the
user first:
`sudo mkdir -p /opt/biomanager && sudo chown "$USER" /opt/biomanager`.
With `TLS=internal`, every device must trust Caddy's root once:
`docker compose exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt > biomanager-root.crt`,
then install it (macOS Keychain "Always Trust"; Windows "Trusted Root
Certification Authorities"; iOS profile + Certificate Trust Settings;
Android "CA certificate"). Docker publishes 80 and 443 on the machine
itself; a network firewall run by IT must let 443 through from the lab
network (and the VPN). Put `BACKUP_DIR` on a second disk if there is one.
A NAS with Docker (fnOS and the like) works as B: Docker is already there,
its own web pages usually hold 80 and 443, and `host/ports.sh` moves
BioManager to a free port (4443) by itself; open that port, not 443,
in any firewall. Its storage volume (e.g. `/vol1/…`) is a good `BACKUP_DIR`.

## Option E: a domain

As D, but: a DNS A record `biomanager.<domain>` → the VM's public IP;
inbound TCP 80 and 443 allowed in the cloud firewall (ask first); `.env`
with `DOMAIN=biomanager.<domain>`, `TLS=acme`, `ACME_EMAIL=<their email>`,
no `COMPOSE_FILE`. On Cloudflare DNS, the record must be "DNS only", not
proxied. Check: `docker compose logs caddy | grep "certificate obtained"`
shows `certificate obtained successfully`; `curl -fsS https://biomanager.<domain>/healthz`
from anywhere prints `ok`. Recommend Google or Microsoft sign-in
(`deploy/README.md`, "Signing in with Google or Microsoft") and strong
passwords, since the sign-in page is public.

Cloudflare Tunnel (not packaged; only if they ask): `cloudflared` on the
host pointing at `https://localhost:443` with `originServerName: <DOMAIN>`
(or `noTLSVerify: true` with `TLS=internal`), and Cloudflare Access in
front. Then no inbound ports are needed.

## Moving the desktop app's data in

Only into a **new, empty** server, before its first `docker compose up`
(after `host/load-image.sh` and with `.env` filled in). The app's folder:
macOS `~/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/`, Windows
`%APPDATA%\Biomanager\`, Linux `~/.local/share/Biomanager/`. The database
is `data/biomanager.db` inside it, and the uploaded files are `uploads/`.
The person quits the app and copies both to the server, e.g. from a Mac:

```bash
scp "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/data/biomanager.db" <user>@<server>:/tmp/lab.db
scp -r "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/uploads" <user>@<server>:/tmp/lab-uploads
```

Then, on the server in the deploy folder:

```bash
docker compose up -d db
docker compose run --rm --no-deps -v /tmp/lab.db:/import/lab.db:ro app \
  sh -c 'python scripts/migrate-to-postgres.py --dry-run /import/lab.db "$DATABASE_URL"'
# if the dry run is clean, the same without --dry-run, then:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose cp /tmp/lab-uploads/. app:/data/uploads/
```

Check: the person signs in with their existing account (no setup code: the
accounts came along) and sees their data. Then D5 (host extras).

## Updating a running server

Once `host/install.sh` has run, an admin can do it in the app: **Settings →
Devices & copies → Updates → Update now** (the server tells its admins when a
release is out). From a shell, `sudo host/update.sh` does the same: backup,
download and SHA-256 check, image, unpack, restart, health check. If this
server's version is older than the first with Update now, do it by hand once,
then run `sudo host/install.sh`:

```bash
cd /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy
docker compose exec backup backup.sh
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/b.tar.gz https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz
tar -xzf /tmp/b.tar.gz -C /opt/biomanager      # .env and backups are not in the bundle
host/load-image.sh && docker compose up -d --build
sudo host/install.sh                           # the updater, if this is the first version with it
```

Check: `docker compose ps` healthy; `curl -fsS https://DOMAIN/healthz`
prints `ok`. The database schema updates itself on start; the log then says
`Upgrading the database from … to …`. If it goes wrong: RUNBOOK.md,
"Updating went wrong".

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `permission denied` on the Docker socket | The user isn't in the `docker` group yet: log out and in, or `newgrp docker` |
| `set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env` / `set DOMAIN in .env` | `.env` is missing that value: run the `sed` lines of D4 again, then `docker compose config --quiet` |
| `pull access denied for ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager` | The image wasn't loaded: run `host/load-image.sh` in the deploy folder, then `docker compose up -d` |
| `app` never healthy | `docker compose logs app`. A malformed `DATABASE_URL` usually means `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` has symbols: use hex only, then `docker compose down` (not `-v`) and `up -d` |
| `/healthz` fails but containers are healthy | `docker compose logs caddy`. `TLS=tailscale`: HTTPS Certificates not enabled in the tailnet, or `COMPOSE_FILE` missing. `TLS=acme`: DNS not pointing at the VM yet, or port 80 closed |
| Browser says the certificate isn't trusted (`TLS=internal`) | Install `biomanager-root.crt` on that device |
| No setup code in the log | An account already exists; the code is only for the first one. `docker compose logs app \| grep -i "setup"` |
| Oracle: "Out of host capacity" | Try later, another availability domain, or a smaller shape |
| A VM on Oracle's free tier stopped after days idle | Oracle stops Always Free VMs that look idle for a week: start it again in Compute → Instances (nothing is lost). Upgrading the account to Pay As You Go prevents it and still bills nothing for Always Free resources |
| Phones can't reach it | Tailscale off on the phone (D), not on the lab network (B), or the root certificate not installed (`TLS=internal`) |

## When you are done

Tell the person, in plain words: the address; that the first account is the
admin; where backups are (`/opt/biomanager/backups`, nightly, restore-tested
weekly) and whether off-site is on; the ntfy topic for alerts; how to update
(above); and that `deploy/RUNBOOK.md` in the bundle says what to do when an
alert arrives. Fill in its table at the top (*Where everything is*) with them:
the address, the server and where to start or rebuild it, where backups go,
off-site or not, the ntfy topic; and have them keep a copy somewhere other
than the server. The user guide is https://biomanager.org/guide.
